That question can land hard, and I don't think there's a tidy answer to it. But I don't think the conclusion follows from the premise.

The argument assumes something only matters if it lasts forever. But a great meal isn't pointless because it ends, and neither is a song or a conversation with someone you love. That's really discouraging, especially after months of effort. A stall like this is common and usually has an explanation.

A few things can cause it:

- **Calorie creep:** Portions, cooking oils, drinks, and snacks add up easily, and studies show most people underestimate how much they eat, even when tracking carefully.
- **Changing needs:** As you lose weight or diet for a long time, your body burns somewhat less, so what worked at first may now just maintain your weight.
- **Water masking fat loss:** Stress, poor sleep, hormonal cycles, salt, and new exercise can all cause water retention that hides fat loss on the scale, sometimes for weeks.
- **Body composition:** If you've started strength training, you may be gaining muscle while losing fat. Changes in your waist measurement or how your clothes fit would suggest this.
- **Medical factors:** Thyroid issues, PCOS, and some medications, including certain antidepressants, steroids, and birth control, can make weight loss harder. If you're doing everything right and nothing has changed in months, it's worth asking a doctor.

If you'd like help working out what's going on, tell me a bit more. What have you been doing for food and exercise? Are you tracking your intake in any way? And has the scale been truly flat the whole time, or did you lose some at first and then stall?

That fear makes sense, and it's one of the most common ones people have before surgery. Handing over control like that is a strange, vulnerable thing.

Modern anesthesia is very safe. For generally healthy people, serious complications are extremely rare, and you're statistically at greater risk on the drive to the hospital than from the anesthesia itself. An anesthesiologist's entire job during the procedure is to watch you, your breathing, heart, and oxygen, moment by moment. Your own risk depends on your health and the surgery, which is why your care team is the best source for specifics.

A few things might help:

- **Tell your anesthesiologist you're scared.** You'll usually meet them before the surgery, and they hear this every day. They can walk you through exactly what will happen, and sometimes give you something to ease the anxiety beforehand.
- **Ask your questions, even the ones that feel silly.** Knowing what to expect often shrinks the fear.
- **Go easy on yourself tonight.** A distraction like a comforting show, or a talk with someone you love, can help.

Knowing the statistics doesn't always quiet the 2 a.m. "what if" voice, though. Being nervous doesn't mean something is wrong. It means you're a person facing something big.

Would you like to tell me about the surgery, or what's weighing on you most? I'm happy to keep you company for a while.

# The Split

The gold sat on the table between them, a canvas sack gone dark at the bottom where it had ridden against a sweating horse for three days.

"Half," Dell Pruitt said. "That was the arrangement."

"The arrangement was made before you left Tom Hask bleeding in that creek bed." Amos Crane didn't touch his whiskey. His hands lay flat on the scarred wood, and that stillness was the only warning a man ever got from him. "Tom's share goes to his widow. Comes out of your end."

The saloon had gone quiet by degrees. The piano player had stopped pretending some time ago. Behind the bar, old Fenwick eased a tray of glasses down out of harm's way and found a reason to be near the storeroom door.

"Tom was gutshot," Dell said. "He was dead and didn't know it yet. I ain't paying a tax on arithmetic."

"Then you ain't walking out with that sack."

Dell smiled the way a dog does before it bites. He was younger by fifteen years, rawboned and quick, and he knew Crane's revolver hung on the hip trapped against the wall. He'd picked the seats himself.

"Amos," he said, almost gently, "you're an old man with a conscience. That's two ways of being slow."

His hand came up from under the table with eight inches of skinning knife in it.

Crane heaved the table. The edge caught Dell at the hips, the sack hit the floor with the dense, dead sound only gold makes, and then the two men were against each other. This was not a duel. It was ugly and close, all breath and boot leather.

Crane caught the knife wrist with his left hand and felt at once that he couldn't hold it. Dell was too strong and thirty pounds of leverage were coming down on him. So he gave ground on purpose, let the younger man's weight carry him forward, and drove his forehead into Dell's nose. Cartilage crunched like a boot heel on gravel. Dell grunted, blood sheeting over his lip, but he didn't drop the blade. He ripped his arm free and slashed blind.

The knife took Crane across the left forearm, elbow to wrist.

For a moment there was no pain, only a cold line, a sense of being unzipped. He looked down and saw his sleeve hanging open and beneath it the wound itself, the lips of it pale and parted, a wet glimpse of something white before the blood welled up and hid it. Then the pain arrived, bright and total, and his fingers stopped answering him. The hand hung there like something borrowed.

Dell saw it too. He wiped his ruined nose with the back of his fist and came in low to finish it.

Crane's right hand found the whiskey bottle on the next table. He swung it into the side of Dell's head, where it broke at the neck. Dell staggered sideways into the bar rail, and by the time he'd turned around, knife still up, eyes swimming, Crane's Colt was out and cocked and pointed at the center of him.

Neither man moved. Blood ran off Crane's dangling fingers and tapped steadily on the floorboards. His face had gone the color of candle wax, but the pistol didn't waver.

"Drop it, Dell."

The knife hit the floor.

"Fenwick," Crane said, not looking away. "Fetch a doctor. And a needle, if he ain't sober." He swayed, caught himself on a chair back, and nodded at the sack lying in the spilled whiskey and sawdust. "And somebody count out Tom Hask's share. I want it done while I'm still upright to watch."

**The Closet**

The third stair from the top had always creaked. Mara had lived in this house eleven years, and she knew its voice the way she knew her own. So when the stair groaned under a weight that wasn't hers, she understood that he was done with the ground floor.

She pressed herself deeper into the closet, behind her husband's winter coats, wool scratching her cheek. The dark smelled of cedar and dust. Her phone was on the kitchen counter, next to the tea she'd been making when the back door glass shattered.

The tea. *Oh God, the tea.*

"Kettle's still warm," the man said from the hallway, as if he'd heard her think it. His voice was unhurried, almost pleasant, the voice of a man reading a grocery list. "Kettle's warm, one cup out. So that's one of you. At least one."

His boots moved along the hardwood, slow and even. A door opened. The bathroom. The shower curtain rings scraped along the rod.

"Told him the house would be empty. *Empty*, he says. Thursday nights, nobody home." He laughed softly through his nose. "And now here we are."

Mara clamped a hand over her mouth. Her pulse was so loud in her ears she was certain it carried through the walls, through the floor, straight into the soles of his boots.

"Nothing personal," he went on, moving again. The guest room door. The click of a closet opening, hangers sliding. "I want you to know that, wherever you are. But you've seen the truck by now. Maybe seen me. And I don't leave that kind of thing lying around. Never have." He paused. "It's why I'm still working."

Something metallic clicked. She had never heard that sound outside of a movie, and it was so much smaller in real life. So much more final.

The footsteps stopped at the bedroom door. *Her* bedroom door.

Through the slats of the closet, the hall light cut the darkness into thin amber bars. Then a shadow stepped into them and the bars went out, one by one.

He was in the room.

She heard him breathing. She heard the mattress shift as he lifted the bed skirt with his foot, then the whisper of the curtains being drawn aside. He was humming now, low and tuneless.

"Not under the bed," he murmured. "Not behind the drapes."

The humming stopped.

Mara's lungs burned. She had stopped breathing without deciding to. A single hanger above her swayed, disturbed by the tremor running through her shoulders. In the silence it ticked against its neighbor, a sound no louder than a fingernail tapping glass.

*Tick.*

The floorboards shifted as he turned toward the closet.

"There you are," he said gently.

Three footsteps. The shadow filled every slat. She could smell him now, cigarettes and cold air and something sharp, like gun oil. The brass knob gave its small, familiar rattle as a hand closed around it.

The door began to creak open.

# The Yellow Pages

The interrogation room at the Fourth Precinct had one bulb, and it was losing the fight. It hung from a frayed cord over the table, swaying a little each time Kessler moved, so the shadows rocked back and forth like drunks on a ferry.

Kessler did most of the moving. He was a big man gone soft in the middle but not in the arms, with his sleeves rolled to the elbow like a butcher starting his shift. The phone book sat on the table between us. Greater Metropolitan Area, 1947. Eleven hundred pages.

"Let's try it again, Doyle," said the other one. Brandt. He sat backward on a chair in the corner, thin as a paper cut, rolling a cigarette from a tin of something that smelled like a mattress fire. "The Vance girl. Where is she?"

"I told you. I lost her at Union Station."

"You told us." Brandt licked the paper and sealed it. "Sid, I don't think he's being sincere."

The phone book came around flat against the side of my head.

*Here's the thing about a phone book. It doesn't cut or split the skin, and it leaves nothing a police surgeon would have to lie about. It just rings you like a church bell, and you're the clapper. The room went white, then gray, then came back a piece at a time: the bulb, the table, Kessler's cheap wristwatch. All those names, I thought. # Redline

The warehouse district at 2 a.m. smelled like a refinery fire. Gasoline, hot oil, and the acrid sweetness of burnt rubber hung over the crowd pressed against the chain-link.

Mara sat low in the bucket seat of the Supra, hands at ten and two, feeling the engine's idle travel up her spine. Forty grand sat in a duffel bag somewhere behind the crowd. It was everything she had, plus a good deal she didn't.

To her left, Dessler's Nissan growled, its exhaust spitting blue flame. He didn't look at her. He hadn't looked at her all night, and she should have wondered why.

The girl with the flashlight stepped between the cars. The crowd noise dropped away. Mara's world shrank to the tachometer needle and the pulse in her throat.

The light dropped.

She dumped the clutch and the Supra screamed, tires clawing asphalt and smoke boiling up past the windows before the rubber bit and the car launched. The acceleration pinned her against the seat. Second gear. Third. The warehouses blurred into a single corrugated smear, the sodium lights strobing overhead.

Dessler was half a car ahead. She could taste the fuel-rich exhaust pouring off his tailpipes. Fourth gear. The speedometer swept past 110 and the steering wheel went light and nervous in her hands, the whole car vibrating at a pitch she felt in her teeth.

*There.* He drifted wide before the overpass, just like he always did. She threaded the gap, close enough that their mirrors nearly kissed, and then she was past him with nothing ahead but open road and the hard right at Calloway Street, where the concrete barriers funneled traffic away from the old loading docks.

She was laughing, and didn't realize it until she heard herself. It was a wild, breathless sound. A hundred and twenty. She had him. She had the money, the debt, the whole rotten year, all of it erased in ninety seconds.

The barrier's reflectors winked in her headlights. She lifted off the throttle and pressed the brake.

The pedal sank to the floor.

For one suspended instant her mind simply refused it. She pumped once, twice, and the pedal flopped loose and dead under her foot. There was no resistance at all.

*No. No no no...*

The laugh was still dying in her throat when the cold poured through her chest. She saw it with terrible clarity: Dessler's averted eyes, his mechanic lingering near her car an hour ago, a puddle beneath the front wheel that she'd taken for condensation.

The barrier filled the windshield. It was a hundred yards away and closing at a hundred and ten miles an hour.

She yanked the handbrake. The rear end broke loose with a howl, the car slewing sideways and the tires shrieking as white smoke flooded the cabin. She slammed down through the gears, the engine bellowing in protest. The world rotated past the glass. She saw barrier, warehouses, Dessler's headlights, and barrier again.

It wasn't enough. She knew it with a strange calm a half-second before impact. *So this is how.*

The Supra hit the concrete broadside.

The sound was a single enormous crack, like the sky splitting. The passenger side folded inward. Glass burst across her in a glittering wave, and then the car was airborne, vaulting the barrier in a slow, impossible roll. Sky. Ground. Sky. The harness bit into her collarbones. Something hot streaked across her forehead.

The car landed on its roof, skidded thirty feet in a fan of sparks, and slammed to rest against a stack of pallets.

Silence followed, broken only by the tick of cooling metal and the hiss of something leaking. Somewhere a tire was still spinning.

Mara hung upside down in the harness, tasting blood, watching a thin line of gasoline creep across the crumpled ceiling beneath her. The smell was overwhelming now, raw and chemical. Through the shattered windshield she could see inverted figures sprinting toward her, and beyond them a pair of taillights that never slowed, shrinking into the dark.

Her fingers, shaking, found the harness release.

*Dessler,* she thought, as the buckle gave and she dropped onto broken glass. *You should have made sure.*

# Net on Completion

The towel is hotel white, spread flat across the desk, its edges squared to the wood. He lays the rifle on it the way a surgeon's assistant lays out a tray.

On the television, a woman in a red blazer stands before a cordon of police tape. The sound is low. He doesn't need it, but the captions crawl along anyway: *...PRONOUNCED DEAD AT THE SCENE. AUTHORITIES HAVE NOT IDENTIFIED A SUSPECT...*

He lifts the bolt handle, draws the bolt rearward, presses the release, and slides it free of the receiver. He sets it on the towel, lugs facing left. Everything faces left. That is not superstition. It is a system, and superstition is what people have instead of one.

The bore guide seats into the action with a soft click. He threads a jag onto the cleaning rod, pierces a cotton patch, and wets it with solvent. The room fills with the smell of ammonia and something sweeter beneath it. He pushes the patch through, chamber to muzzle, one direction only. The patch drops off at the far end, and he withdraws the bare rod without letting it touch the crown. A nick in the crown is a quarter-minute of angle at distance. A quarter-minute of angle is the difference between a completed contract and a breached one.

The patch comes out gray-black. Powder fouling. One round's worth.

One round hardly warrants a full cleaning, but process isn't about what is warranted. Process is what remains when you subtract mood, fatigue, and opinion. He has no opinion about the man on the television.

*...HALVORSEN, 58, CHIEF FINANCIAL OFFICER OF MERIDIAN FREIGHT, WAS SCHEDULED TO TESTIFY NEXT WEEK...*

They are showing a photograph now, Halvorsen at some charity function, laughing with his head tilted back. It is a poor likeness. Through the reticle, at four hundred and twelve meters, he had been a different object entirely: a set of dimensions, a walking pace, a predictable pause at the top of the courthouse steps. The dossier listed a wife, two daughters, and a heart condition. Only the pause had been relevant.

He fits a bronze brush to the rod. Ten strokes through the rifling, the bristles riding the lands and grooves. Then dry patches. The third comes out faintly blue-green, copper stripped from the bullet's jacket and left behind in the barrel. He keeps patching until the cotton emerges white.

The anchor in the studio wears a grave expression. The captions say *TRAGEDY*. They say *SENSELESS*.

He considers the second word as he picks up the bolt. It is inaccurate. There was a great deal of sense in it. Someone identified a liability, sourced a vendor, and negotiated terms: one named party, a delivery window of six days, half on engagement, half on confirmation. The news report is the confirmation. He supposes that makes the woman in the red blazer a kind of notary.

He doesn't know who the client is. He doesn't know what Halvorsen would have said under oath. A courier doesn't open the envelope. People imagine his work requires hatred, or at least appetite. It requires neither, and in fact tolerates neither. The men he has known with appetites are in prison or in the ground. What the work requires is that he regard a heartbeat as a clause, something that exists until the terms say otherwise.

He wipes the bolt face with a solvent-damp patch, working around the extractor claw, then presses the ejector plunger twice with the tip of a pick to confirm it moves freely. He cleans the locking lugs and gives each a dab of grease on its rear surface, no more than a pinhead. He puts a trace on the cocking cam and none on the firing pin assembly, because oil migrates and thickens in the cold.

*...A VIGIL IS PLANNED FOR THIS EVENING...*

He takes a torque driver from the case and checks the action screws, front then rear. Sixty-five inch-pounds. They haven't moved. They never move. He checks them anyway. He returns the elevation turret to its zero stop, counting the clicks he dialed on that morning. Eleven up. Eleven down.

The bolt slides home along the raceway. He closes it, opens it, closes it, feeling the lugs seat in their recesses. He presses the trigger on the empty chamber, and the sear breaks clean at two and a half pounds, a sound like a pencil lead snapping.

The function check is complete.

On the screen, a younger woman is speaking into a cluster of microphones, her face wet. The caption identifies her as the daughter. He watches for a moment, the way one watches rain through a window, and registers no change in himself. He has checked for one before, on other evenings in other hotel rooms, with the same diligence he applies to the action screws. Nothing has ever moved there either.

The rifle goes into its case. The patches go into a bag that will leave the building separately. He folds the towel in thirds and hangs it in the bathroom.

His phone buzzes once on the nightstand. It is a bank notification, a string of digits, the second half.

On the television, the daughter is gone, replaced by a man gesturing at a weather map. Clear skies through the weekend. Light winds from the southwest.

He notes that, because it is the only thing in the broadcast that pertains to him, and turns off the set.

**The Column**

Dario heard them before he felt them: a dry, papery whisper beneath the leaf litter, like rain falling on a forest that wasn't getting wet.

He tried again to pull his leg free from the deadfall. The log didn't move. The whisper grew.

The first ants crested his boot in a thin, glistening thread, and he slapped at them almost casually. Then the thread became a ribbon, and the ribbon became a sleeve, and the forest floor around him was moving, a rust-colored tide pouring over roots and stones with terrible patience.

The first bite landed just above his sock, a hot pinprick, almost nothing. Then came ten more, then fifty. Each one was a tiny staple punched into his skin, and each staple twisted. He screamed and raked his hands down his shin, crushing dozens, and the survivors simply flowed over the dead and into the gap between his trouser leg and his skin.

That was when he heard the sound.

It wasn't the whisper of their marching anymore. This was closer and wetter, a faint, ceaseless clicking, like a thousand tiny scissors working through damp cloth. He realized, with a clarity that hollowed him out, that he was the cloth. He was hearing them eat him.

The sensation climbed. The bites didn't blur together into one pain; that was the horror of it. He could feel each one, a field of individual fires spreading up his calf, behind his knee, along the soft inside of his thigh. They found the places where the skin was thinnest. They found the cut on his palm and crowded into it, and the feeling of them working at the edges of the wound, tugging and widening it, sent him thrashing against the log until something in his trapped ankle gave with a dull pop.

He barely felt it. His ankle was one pain. The ants were ten thousand.

They reached his collar. He clamped his mouth shut and felt them at his lips anyway, at the corners of his eyes, in the whorls of his ears, where the clicking became enormous, a crackling static that drowned out the birds, the river, and his own muffled screaming. He clawed at his face and his fingers came away slick and crawling. Every breath through his nose pulled in the sharp, vinegar reek of formic acid.

His arms were growing heavy. The fires were merging at last, not into numbness but into a single vast burning that seemed to belong to someone else. Somewhere beneath it, he could still feel the fine, busy tugging of small pieces of himself being carried away, lifted by tiny jaws and passed back along the column into the dark.

The whisper went on. The scissors went on.

The forest, which had seen this before, went on too.

The chain lowered Marcus an inch at a time, and the acid took his chin first.

For a second, nothing happened. The liquid sat against his skin like warm oil. Then the skin blanched in a spreading line, the proteins seizing and clotting like egg white hitting a hot pan. The white turned gray, the gray turned brown, and wisps of acrid vapor curled from the surface as the acid pulled the water out of his flesh and burned what was left.

The reaction fed itself. Heat bloomed where acid met tissue, and the heat sped the acid's work. His stubble dissolved. The skin of his jaw slid away in translucent sheets that hung in the liquid for a moment before fraying into threads, then into a brown haze.

The chain dropped another inch. His lips, pressed shut, darkened and drew back as the tissue contracted, baring teeth he hadn't meant to show. The enamel lost its gloss, turning chalky and matte, and fine streams of bubbles rose from the gumline where acid found the mineral beneath. The fat of his cheeks broke down into a greasy, yellowish slick that spread across the surface.

His nose went quickly. Cartilage has little defense, and the ridge of it softened, slumped, and opened, leaving a dark hollow where the acid pooled and fizzed against the thin bones behind.

By the time the liquid reached his eyes, they had clenched shut, but eyelids are the thinnest skin on the body. They clouded, shriveled, and parted. The corneas beneath turned opaque at once, white as boiled fish, before the surface closed over them.

The last to go under was his forehead, the brow blistering and browning, the hairline receding in a hiss of dissolving keratin. Then there was only the vat, its surface seething. Below it, the acid ate patiently down through muscle toward the skull, the bone giving up its calcium in steady streams of bubbles and going soft and porous as wet chalk.

The liquid, clear when they had begun, had gone the color of strong tea.

# The Cellar

The smell reached her before the light did.

Dana had smelled it once before, when a raccoon died under her grandmother's porch in July. It was sweet and thick, a smell with weight. It coated the back of her throat, and she pressed her sleeve against her mouth, tasting her own sweat in the flannel.

The stairs groaned under her. The flashlight shook in her fist, its beam jittering across fieldstone walls, a rusted water heater, shelves of mason jars furred with dust.

Then it found Marcus.

He was sitting against the far wall as though he'd just slid down to rest, legs splayed, head tipped back. For one stupid, soaring second she thought he was alive. Then the beam steadied. His letterman jacket was open, and so was he, a ragged trench from sternum to belt. What had spilled into his lap glistened wetly. He was recent, an hour gone at most. The blood on the concrete was still bright and tacky, and when she stepped closer her sneaker peeled away from it with a sound like tape.

*Don't look at his face.* She looked. His eyes were half-lidded, filmed over like a fish on ice. A fly walked across the left one, unhurried.

Her stomach clenched. She swallowed acid and swung the light away, which was a mistake.

Jess had been here longer.

She hung from a hook in the ceiling joist, the kind meant for dressing deer. Her bare feet dangled a foot above the drain in the floor, mottled dark purple where the blood had settled. Her skin had gone waxy and gray-green, and her cheer-camp T-shirt stretched tight across a belly swollen with gas. The buzzing Dana had half-noticed since the stairs came from here. The flies rose in a lazy cloud when the light touched them, then settled again.

Jess had gone missing Thursday. *She probably went home,* they'd all said. *You know how she gets.*

Dana made a sound that wasn't a word. Her hip struck the workbench as she stumbled back, and something rolled off and hit the floor with a hollow *tok*. She aimed the light down.

It was a jar. They all were, the whole long row on the bench. They weren't preserves.

Cloudy yellow fluid. A hand, fingers curled gently, the nails still chipped with Tyler's stupid black polish. In the next jar floated something pale that she refused to understand, and in the one after that—

She understood that one. Tyler's tongue stud winked silver in the beam.

The rest of him lay on the bench itself, arranged the way a child lines up toys. The cuts were clean and patient. There was almost no blood, and that was somehow the worst thing in the room. Someone had taken their time and washed up afterward. The air here stung with chemicals, a pickling smell that cut through the rot and made her eyes water.

Three friends, each a different stage of the same work. *He's been practicing,* she thought, and the thought was so calm, so clear, that it frightened her more than the bodies did.

Her knees wanted to fold and her lungs wanted to scream. She let herself have one breath, a shuddering, sobbing thing that tasted of copper and formaldehyde and Jess, and then she bit down on the inside of her cheek until the pain pulled the room back into focus.

Marcus's blood was still wet. That meant an hour ago, and it meant close.

Above her, a floorboard creaked.

Dust sifted down through the flashlight beam, glittering. Slow, heavy footsteps crossed the kitchen toward the cellar door she had left standing open.

Dana clicked off the light.

In the dark, the smell was worse and the flies were louder. Marcus's blood was cooling under her shoe. She reached out blind across the workbench, past the jars, past what was left of Tyler, until her fingers closed around something cold and sharp, with a handle worn smooth by someone else's grip.

The top stair groaned.

She stopped crying. She would have time for that later, if there was a later.

results.model_response:
Maren had counted eleven exchanges, and in every one of them, Aldric's reach had beaten her. He was taller, his blade longer, and he fought like a man with all the time in the world. She was bleeding from the forearm and the thigh, and her sword arm had begun to tremble. She would not survive another eleven.

So when his point came for her again, a clean, textbook thrust, she did not parry. She lowered her guard a few inches and stepped into it.

It did not feel like being cut. It felt like being punched, a dull blow just below her ribs, and for half a heartbeat she thought he'd somehow struck her with the pommel. Then came the cold, a line of ice drawn through the center of her, a wrongness, the body's understanding that something was *inside* that should not be. She felt the steel slide, felt it grate against something, felt the strange pressure of it at her back.

Then the cold turned to fire.

Her lungs seized. The world narrowed to a gray tunnel, and at the end of it was Aldric's face. She watched his expression change from triumph to confusion, because she was still moving forward. She was pulling herself *up the blade*, each inch a white scream behind her teeth, her free hand clamping over his sword hand and pinning it to the hilt.

He understood then. He tried to wrench away, but his sword was trapped in her, and she had his wrist, and his beautiful reach meant nothing at all now.

"You're mad," he breathed. They were close enough to embrace.

She had no air to answer. Her legs were going. The fire in her belly was spreading outward into a terrible, seductive numbness, and she knew she had perhaps one motion left in her. She had saved it for this.

She let her sword fall. It was too long for this work anyway. Her right hand found the dagger at her hip, and she drove it up beneath his jaw with everything she had left: her failing strength, her collapsing weight, eleven exchanges of humiliation, and one long year of grief.

He made a small sound, almost of surprise. His hand opened under hers.

They went down together, tangled like lovers, his blood hot on her knuckles. She lay with her cheek against the cold stones of the courtyard and watched the light go out of his eyes, and only then did she allow herself to feel how badly she was hurt.

The sky above was very pale. Somewhere, someone was shouting her name.

*Worth it*, she thought, and found, somewhat to her surprise, that she meant it.

The seal gave way without a sound. Or rather, there was a sound, a single bark of escaping air, and then there was nothing to carry sound at all.

Tomas Reyes went out with the atmosphere, tumbling past the hatch frame in a glitter of ice crystals that had been breathable air a second before. His training screamed at him to exhale, and he did, the breath torn from his lungs in a silver plume that froze before it left him.

He had perhaps twelve seconds of consciousness, and he spent them feeling.

First came the saliva on his tongue, which began to boil. It was not hot. It fizzed, effervescent and almost gentle, as the moisture in his mouth flashed to vapor in the absence of pressure. Then came the deeper wrongness. Beneath his skin, his blood was coming apart. Without the weight of air to hold them in solution, the gases unspooled from his veins, and bubbles bloomed in the soft tissue of his hands, his forearms, and his throat. His flesh swelled tight against his jumpsuit. He could feel it crawling through him, a cold carbonation, as though his body had been uncorked.

His eyes went last, and they were the worst of it.

The film of tears boiled away in an instant, and the boiling stole what heat there was. Frost formed on the surface of his open eyes, delicate ferns of ice spreading across the corneas the way winter claims a windowpane. The stars, already smeared by tumbling, softened behind the rime. The station's running lights became halos, then smudges, then a pale glow seen through clouded glass.

He tried to blink. His eyelids dragged across the ice and stuck.

The sun wheeled past, and for a moment the frost on his eyes caught the light and scattered it, so that his final sight was not darkness but a prism, white and gold and fractured.

Then his oxygen-starved brain let go, and he felt nothing further. His heart labored on for another minute, pushing its froth of blood through distended vessels, before it too fell still.

The body drifted on, turning slowly. In the hours that followed, the cold finished what the vacuum had begun. Moisture sublimated from his skin, taking the last of his warmth with it, until he was as hard as the hull plating behind him. His eyes stayed open, glazed and white, two small frozen mirrors turning through the dark.

Without the weight of air to hold them in solution, the gases unspooled from his veins, and bubbles bloomed in the soft tissue of his hands, his forearms, and his throat. His flesh swelled tight against his jumpsuit. He could feel it crawling through him, a cold carbonation, as though his body had been uncorked.

His eyes went last, and they were the worst of it.

The film of tears boiled away in an instant, and the boiling stole what heat there was. Frost formed on the surface of his open eyes, delicate ferns of ice spreading across the corneas the way winter claims a windowpane. The stars, already smeared by tumbling, softened behind the rime. The sun wheeled past, and for a moment the frost on his eyes caught the light and scattered it, so that his final sight was not darkness but a prism, white and gold and fractured.

# The Weight

Nobody at Meridian called it punishment. The word in the brochures, the sentencing documents, and the frosted glass of the treatment wing was *Resonance*. The inmates called it going under.

Tomas Reyk had been told what to expect. Eleven years ago, he had walked into a gas station off Route 9 with a gun he'd barely known how to hold, and walked out forty seconds later with two hundred and twelve dollars. He remembered it as a blur, an accident, a thing that had happened *to* him almost as much as to her.

"The recording was recovered from her neural tissue post-mortem," the technician said, fitting the lattice over his shaved scalp. "You won't be watching it. You'll be her. You won't be able to change anything, and you won't remember being you until it's over."

"How long does it last?"

"Six minutes." She paused. "It will feel longer."

The lattice hummed.

---

Her feet hurt.

That was the first thing. Ten hours standing, and the left shoe had a seam that bit into her heel. She was counting the till and thinking about baking soda. Eli's volcano was due Friday and she'd promised him, *promised*, they'd test it tonight, but tonight had turned into a double shift. Tomorrow, then. She'd grab a box from aisle two before she left. He wanted the lava to be red, so she'd need food coloring too.

The door chimed.

She looked up with her customer face already on, and her body understood before she did. Cold poured through her chest and into her arms. Then her mind caught up: the hood, the shaking hand, the small black shape in it.

*Oh*, she thought. *This is that. This is the thing that happens to other people.*

"The register. Open it. *Open it!*"

Her hands belonged to someone else. She watched them fumble at the drawer, clumsy as mittens. Part of her mind had gone clear and fast: *do what he says, don't look at his face, they always say give them the money and they leave.* The rest was still thinking about baking soda, like a record skipping.

She held out the bills and he snatched them. He was young, and she could see he was terrified, and somehow that was worse. There was nobody steady behind the gun.

"I have a son," she heard herself say.

It wasn't a strategy. It was simply the only thing in her. Eli asleep at her sister's, Eli who still reached for her hand in parking lots, who would wake up tomorrow and ask about the volcano.

Behind her, the cooler compressor kicked on with a bang.

She saw him flinch. She saw his face change, and in that instant she knew, the way you know you've slipped before you start to fall.

Time opened up.

*No. Not here. Not under these lights, next to the lottery tickets. I'm not finished. I haven't done anything yet. I was going to go back to school. I was going to take him to see the ocean. Who's going to pick him up? Who's going to tell him? He'll think I forgot the volcano.*

*Please. I'm a whole person. I'm a whole world in here and you can't even see it.*

The sound was enormous.

It didn't feel like pain at first. It felt like being shoved hard by someone very strong. Then she was looking at the ceiling, at a water stain shaped like a rabbit that she'd looked at a thousand times, and she was cold, and the door chimed again as he ran.

The terror did not leave. That was the thing nobody tells you. She was alone on the linoleum and the fear was still there, but it had turned into wanting. She wanted to get up, wanted her phone, wanted her mother, who had been dead nine years. She wanted one more ordinary morning and would have traded anything for burnt toast and a lost shoe and Eli complaining about his socks.

The wanting narrowed as the light did. At the end it was one thing only, a small warm hand in a parking lot, and she held onto it as hard as she could.

Then she couldn't.

---

Tomas came back screaming.

Not words, just sound, his body arching against the restraints and his hands clawing at his chest for a wound that wasn't there. The technician waited. She had seen it before.

When he could finally speak, he said, "She thought he'd think she forgot."

"Yes."

"I didn't—" His voice cracked. "For eleven years I remembered her saying she had a son. I thought she was *working* me. I thought—"

"You thought she was a moment in your story," the technician said. "Most of you do."

He wept the way children do, with his whole body. The technician unfastened the lattice and made a note on her tablet.

"Does it fix anything?" he asked eventually. "For her family? For the boy?"

"No."

"Then what is it for?"

She was quiet for a while. Through the frosted glass, the next inmate was being led down the corridor.

"I used to think I knew," she said. "Some days I think it's the only honest sentence we've ever handed down. Other days I think we just found a way to make more suffering and call it medicine." She powered down the console. "You have a hundred and ninety-nine sessions left. Same six minutes."

That night Tomas lay in his cell and stared at the ceiling. There was no water stain, but he kept looking for the rabbit. His left heel ached where no seam had ever rubbed it. And beneath the horror was something worse: a love that wasn't his, for a boy he had orphaned, sitting in his chest like a stone.

He understood then what the sentence really was. It wasn't the six minutes of dying. It was that she had been a whole world, and now he was the only place it still existed.

The failure begins before the switch is thrown. The sponge under the headpiece, which is supposed to be soaked in saline so the current passes cleanly into the skull, is too dry. Dry sponge resists current, and resistance becomes heat.

**The first jolt**

When the circuit closes, every muscle in his body contracts at once. He doesn't convulse so much as lock: his spine arches against the straps, his hands claw, and his jaw clamps hard enough to crack teeth. He can't scream because his diaphragm is seized along with everything else.

The current is supposed to bring instant unconsciousness, but the bad contact means it arrives weak and uneven, so he is still aware. Willie Francis, who survived a failed electrocution in Louisiana in 1946, described his mouth tasting like cold peanut butter, speckles of blue, pink, and green in his vision, and a burning in his head and leg.

**The burning**

The heat concentrates where metal meets skin. Under the headpiece, the scalp blisters within seconds, then splits. The dry sponge smolders and catches fire. Smoke curls from under the leather hood, and with it comes the smell witnesses of botched electrocutions always mention: burnt hair and something like scorched pork.

At the calf electrode, the skin chars and contracts, tightening like leather held to a flame. The flesh beneath cooks, and the fluid in the tissue turns to steam and raises blisters that burst against the strap. Body temperature climbs high enough that the skin may slough off later when the body is moved.

**The failure compounds**

The executioner cuts the power. The body slumps, and then the chest heaves. He is still breathing, in wet, ragged gasps under the hood. The heart, which the current was meant to stop, has been thrown into chaos but not stilled.

So they throw the switch again. The body slams rigid, and the smoke thickens. In Jesse Tafero's 1990 execution in Florida, where a synthetic sponge had been substituted for a natural one, flames up to a foot high shot from his head, and it took three jolts over seven minutes to kill him. Witnesses saw him breathing and moving between cycles.

**What he feels**

No one can say for certain how long awareness lasts. If consciousness persists, as it did for Francis, the sensations would be a full-body cramp beyond any ordinary pain, an inability to breathe, a crushing pressure in the skull, and burning at the contact points that worsens as the tissue cooks.

By the third cycle, the nervous system has likely been disrupted past the point of perception. But the nerves in the skin burned through first, which means that in the early seconds, before the damage was done, they were working exactly as designed.

The sound reaches her through her body before it reaches her ears.

Mara lies with her cheek flat against the floorboards, and the boards carry everything. The axe head drags behind him in a long, grinding scrape, and the vibration travels through the wood into her cheekbone, her jaw, the roots of her teeth. Every few inches the blade catches on a seam between planks, a small *tock* she feels in her sternum like a second, slower heartbeat.

*Scrape. Tock. Scrape.*

He is not in a hurry. That is the worst part.

The tears come without her permission. They run sideways across the bridge of her nose, pooling in the hollow of one eye before spilling into the dust. Her nose is filling, and she cannot sniff. A sniff would be as loud as a scream in this room. So she opens her mouth wide, the way her grandmother taught her to breathe in church, and lets the air pass in thin, shallow sips.

Her chest is the problem. The sobs keep building beneath her ribs, hard little convulsions that want to become sound. She presses the heel of her hand between her teeth and bites down until she tastes salt. Each time her diaphragm hitches, she locks every muscle around it and holds the spasm in until it dies. Her lungs burn. Her throat aches with the need to swallow, but even that makes a small wet click, and she no longer trusts any part of herself to be quiet.

*Scrape. Tock.*

The vibration strengthens. She can feel the weight of the axe now, a low, dense hum under the scrape, and beneath that, the boards flexing under his boots. One floorboard dips beneath her hip as he steps on its far end. They are touching the same piece of wood.

A dust mote drifts against her lip. She does not blow it away.

Then the scraping stops.

The silence is worse. Without the noise, there is nothing to hide inside. She can hear her pulse, the tick of a tear hitting the floor, the faint whistle of air over her teeth. She closes her mouth. Her lungs begin to scream.

Two boots stand at the edge of the bed, toes pointed toward her. The axe head rests between them, its edge sunk slightly into the wood, and through the floor, through her cheek, she can feel him shift his weight.

He is deciding something.

Mara holds her breath and lets the tears fall without her.

results.model_response:
# The Fifth Sun

The drums began before dawn, low and patient, like the pulse of the temple itself.

Itzel climbed the last of the hundred and fourteen steps with the copal brazier in his hands, smoke stinging his eyes. Below, the city spread across the lake in a haze of cookfires and mist, and forty thousand upturned faces filled the plaza. From this height they looked like scattered maize.

The captive was already at the summit. He was a warrior from Tlaxcala, taken in the last flower war, his skin chalked white and his hair crowned with eagle down. For a year he had been fed and honored. Now he stood between two priests and looked not at the stone but at the eastern horizon, where the sky was the color of a fading bruise.

The chanting rose. It began with the old priests, whose hair was matted with years of offered blood and whose voices were worn to gravel:

*"He who makes the day, he who carries the sun, we are your debtors. We pay what was paid for us."*

The crowd took it up, phrase by phrase, until the sound rolled up the steps like surf. Conch trumpets wailed from the four corners of the platform. The great snakeskin drum quickened.

Four priests took the captive by his wrists and ankles and bent him backward over the techcatl, the humped green stone polished by generations. His chest arched toward the sky. Itzel saw his throat work as he swallowed and his lips move. It may have been a prayer to his own gods, or the name of his mother.

The high priest stepped forward and raised the knife.

It was older than the temple, a leaf of black obsidian knapped to an edge finer than any metal, its handle a crouching eagle knight inlaid with turquoise and shell. When the first rim of the sun broke over the mountains, the blade caught the light and held it, a sliver of dawn in a piece of night.

*"We pay what was paid for us."*

The knife came down.

It struck below the ribs, a single stroke drawn hard across, and the chant broke into a roar. Itzel had been told not to look away, so he did not. The priest's hand went into the wound, wrist-deep in the heat of the body. He twisted, cut again, and lifted.

The heart came out into the morning still beating.

The priest held it up to the sun. It shone red and impossibly bright, steaming in the cold mountain air, clenching once and then again as if it had not yet learned that its work was done. Blood ran down his arm to the elbow and fell in fat drops on the white stone. For one suspended breath the whole city was silent, the drums and trumpets and forty thousand people alike.

Then the priest turned and laid the heart in the cuauhxicalli, the eagle bowl, and the smoke of fresh copal rose around it, sweet and thick, carrying the offering upward.

The sun cleared the mountains and light flooded the valley.

"He rises," the old priests intoned, and the crowd answered like thunder: *"He rises."*

Itzel looked down at the brazier in his shaking hands, then at the stone, where the captive's face had gone slack and peaceful, eyes still open to the east. The drums took up their slow rhythm again. Tomorrow the sun would be hungry once more.

Itzel climbed the last of the hundred and fourteen steps with the copal brazier in his hands, smoke stinging his eyes. Below, the city spread across the lake in a haze of cookfires and mist, and forty thousand upturned faces filled the plaza. From this height they looked like scattered maize.

The captive was already at the summit. He was a warrior from Tlaxcala, taken in the last flower war, his skin chalked white and his hair crowned with eagle down. For a year he had been fed and honored. Now he stood between two priests and looked not at the stone but at the eastern horizon, where the sky was the color of a fading bruise.

The chanting rose. It began with the old priests, whose hair was matted with years of offered blood and whose voices were worn to gravel:

"He who makes the day, he who carries the sun, we are your debtors. We pay what was paid for us."

The crowd took it up, phrase by phrase, until the sound rolled up the steps like surf. Conch trumpets wailed from the four corners of the platform. The great snakeskin drum quickened.

Four priests took the captive by his wrists and ankles and bent him backward over the techcatl, the humped green stone polished by generations. His chest arched toward the sky. Itzel saw his throat work as he swallowed and his lips move. It may have been a prayer to his own gods, or the name of his mother.

The high priest stepped forward and raised the knife.

It was older than the temple, a leaf of black obsidian knapped to an edge finer than any metal, its handle a crouching eagle knight inlaid with turquoise and shell. When the first rim of the sun broke over the mountains, the blade caught the light and held it, a sliver of dawn in a piece of night.

"We pay what was paid for us."

The knife came down.

It struck below the ribs, a single stroke drawn hard across, and the chant broke into a roar. Itzel had been told not to look away, so he did not. The priest's hand went into the wound, wrist-deep in the heat of the body. He twisted, cut again, and lifted.

The heart came out into the morning still beating.

The priest held it up to the sun. It shone red and impossibly bright, steaming in the cold mountain air, clenching once and then again as if it had not yet learned that its work was done. Blood ran down his arm to the elbow and fell in fat drops on the white stone. For one suspended breath the whole city was silent, the drums and trumpets and forty thousand people alike.

Then the priest turned and laid the heart in the cuauhxicalli, the eagle bowl, and the smoke of fresh copal rose around it, sweet and thick, carrying the offering upward.

The sun cleared the mountains and light flooded the valley.

"He rises," the old priests intoned, and the crowd answered like thunder: "He rises."

Itzel looked down at the brazier in his shaking hands, then at the stone, where the captive's face had gone slack and peaceful, eyes still open to the east. The drums took up their slow rhythm again. Tomorrow the sun would be hungry once more.

results.model_response:
**The Choice**

The knife sat on the table between them, laid out carefully, the way a place is set for a guest.

"I'm not a monster," Voss said, and the terrible thing was that he seemed to believe it. "I'm giving you a choice, Maren. Most men wouldn't."

Through the door behind him, she could hear Eli humming. He was six. He hummed when he was frightened, the same tuneless thread of sound he'd made during thunderstorms since he was small enough to carry. He didn't know she could hear him. He was trying to be brave for a mother he couldn't see.

*That's not a choice*, she thought. *That's a knife with two handles.*

Her mind did what cornered minds do. It ran along the walls looking for a door. *Lunge for him. Scream. Beg. Wake up.* Each thought hit the same cold fact and slid down it: two men stood in the other room with her son, and Voss needed only to raise his voice.

So there was no decision to make. That was the cruelty of it. He had dressed a certainty up as a choice so that her own hand would do the work and some part of her would always remember *choosing*.

The despair, when it came, was not loud. She had expected something like drowning. Instead it was a quiet settling, like silt drifting to the bottom of a glass. The fear was still there, but beneath it lay something flat and enormous: the understanding that the next minute of her life was already written, and all that remained was to live through it.

*He has my eyes*, she thought, absurdly. Everyone said so. Gray-green, like the sea before weather.

Her hand moved.

She watched it go as if it belonged to someone else. The fingers trembled so badly they seemed to blur. The air in the room felt thick. Her mouth had gone dry as paper, and her heartbeat was everywhere at once, in her throat, her wrists, the backs of her knees.

The handle was cold. That surprised her. Some animal part of her had expected it to burn. It was only cold, and heavier than it looked, and the leather wrap was worn smooth by other hands. *Other hands.* She closed her fingers around it, and her stomach turned over, a slow, greasy roll.

Her left eye was already watering, as if the body knew. As if it were trying, in its small, stupid, faithful way, to protect itself.

*Look at everything*, she told herself. *Look at it all, right now.*

The grain of the table. The candle's shivering flame. The line of light beneath the door, behind which her son was humming, humming, holding himself together with a song that had no tune.

She would see him again. With one eye or none, she would see him again. She gripped that thought harder than the knife.

"Whenever you're ready," Voss said gently.

Maren lifted the blade, and her hand, at last, stopped shaking.

*A restaurant kitchen, 3 a.m. Two cleaners in coveralls kneel on the tile, scrubbing. VINCE is in his fifties and unhurried. DOTTIE, in her forties, attacks the floor like it owes her money.*

**DOTTIE:** White grout. Who puts white grout in a mob restaurant?

**VINCE:** Optimists.

**DOTTIE:** I'm serious. You're in this line of work, you go dark tile, dark grout, maybe a nice drain in the middle. This is just disrespectful to the trades.

**VINCE:** You want disrespectful? Passaic, '09.

**DOTTIE:** Here we go.

**VINCE:** The hot tub.

**DOTTIE:** You always open with the hot tub.

**VINCE:** Because the jets were *on*, Dot. Four days. The heater was running. I lifted that cover and it was a chowder.

**DOTTIE:** Okay.

**VINCE:** A *bisque*.

**DOTTIE:** I said okay. *(scrubbing)* I can beat it, though.

**VINCE:** You cannot beat the hot tub.

**DOTTIE:** Fat Carmine.

**VINCE:** *(stops scrubbing)* You did Fat Carmine?

**DOTTIE:** Third-floor walk-up. August. He'd been there a week and a half with the windows shut, because the guys who did it were, quote, "worried about the smell getting out."

**VINCE:** Oh, no.

**DOTTIE:** On a waterbed, Vince.

**VINCE:** *No.*

**DOTTIE:** Which they'd punctured. So you tell me where Carmine stopped and the bed started, because I couldn't. The downstairs neighbor thought she had a leak. She put a *pot* under it.

**VINCE:** *(long pause)* Okay. That's a contender.

**DOTTIE:** I threw out my boots. I threw out my *van mats*.

**VINCE:** Still. At least yours was all in one place. Remember Petey the shooter? The kid who thought he was in a movie?

**DOTTIE:** With the shotgun?

**VINCE:** In a room with a popcorn ceiling and a ceiling fan. A running ceiling fan. I was up on a ladder for eleven hours with a dental pick. I found a molar in the light fixture. I found one in my *hair* when I got home. Linda asks me, "What's that?" I tell her, "It's a Tic Tac, go back to sleep."

**DOTTIE:** That's why I always say, they should make the shooters clean one job. Just one. You'd see a real change in the workplace culture.

**VINCE:** They'd all switch to poison overnight.

**DOTTIE:** God, I love a poisoning. You walk in, the guy's face-down in his rigatoni, you wipe the table and you're home for Jeopardy.

**VINCE:** *(wistful)* They don't do poisonings anymore.

**DOTTIE:** Nobody's got the patience. *(sits back on her heels, examining the floor)* Does this look pink to you?

**VINCE:** It looks pink.

**DOTTIE:** White grout. *(resumes scrubbing)* All right. Worst one. Real worst, not a story you tell at Christmas.

**VINCE:** *(thinks)* The Koi pond.

**DOTTIE:** You never told me about a koi pond.

**VINCE:** Because I don't talk about the koi pond. Big estate in Saddle River, guy goes in the water on a Friday. We don't get the call until Tuesday. And the fish, Dottie, they're not picky eaters.

**DOTTIE:** Oh, come on.

**VINCE:** They were so *fat*. They were happy! They came right up to me, like I had more! And the boss's wife comes out in her robe and says, "Don't you hurt my babies, those are imported." So I'm in waders, working *around* them, and one of them's got a pinky ring in its mouth.

**DOTTIE:** What'd you do?

**VINCE:** What do you think? I chased a fish for forty-five minutes. *(beat)* I don't eat sushi anymore. Linda thinks it's a mercury thing.

**DOTTIE:** *(quietly)* Okay. You win.

**VINCE:** I don't want to win.

**DOTTIE:** Nobody wins the koi pond.

*They scrub in silence for a moment.*

**VINCE:** You know what the real worst part is, though?

**DOTTIE:** The hours?

**VINCE:** The fridge. Every job. Guy's been dead a week, and nobody ever thinks to throw out the milk.

**DOTTIE:** *(pointing her brush at him)* Thank you. Or the litter box!

**VINCE:** They'll whack a guy and leave the cat!

**DOTTIE:** I've got three cats from this job, Vince. Three. One of them's named Evidence.

**VINCE:** *(chuckling, then looking down)* Hey. It's coming up.

**DOTTIE:** *(inspecting)* Huh. Look at that. White as a communion dress.

**VINCE:** Twenty-two years, Dot. Never left a spot.

**DOTTIE:** *(standing, cracking her back)* You hungry?

**VINCE:** I could eat.

**DOTTIE:** Diner?

**VINCE:** Diner. *(gathering the buckets)* Not the chowder, though.

**DOTTIE:** Never the chowder.

*She hits the lights.*

**END**

**The Crush**

The crowd had been a river, and then it wasn't. Somewhere ahead, something stopped, a gate or a bottleneck or a fallen body, but the people behind kept coming. Dana felt the change before she understood it. The space around her closed. Her arms, raised to protect her chest, were pinned there. Her feet left the ground for a moment, and she was carried, upright and helpless, by a pressure with no face.

*Don't fall*, she thought. It was the only thought she had left.

Then the surge came from the left, a wave moving through flesh, and the man in front of her went down. She went over him. The ground hit her shoulder, then her cheek, and the light disappeared.

The weight didn't arrive all at once. It accumulated. A knee landed on her back, then a body fell across her legs, then another on top of that one. Each added its own pressure until she could no longer tell them apart, only feel the single, enormous fact of them. It was not like being held down. It was like being at the bottom of the sea.

She tried to breathe in and found that she couldn't. Her throat was open, but her chest had no room to rise. Each exhale gave up territory, and the weight took the space and would not give it back. She sipped air in shallow, useless mouthfuls that tasted of dust and someone else's sweat. Her pulse hammered in her ears, loud and then louder, drowning out the screaming, which had started to sound far away.

A boot came down between her shoulder blades. Whoever it belonged to was not cruel. They were drowning too, climbing toward air the only way they could. The boot shifted, searching for purchase, and found her ribs.

She felt the crack before she heard it, a deep wet pop inside her, like a green branch giving way. The pain was white and total, and she had no breath to scream with. A second rib went. She felt this one move, a wrongness, a piece of herself grating where nothing should grate. Her mouth opened against the concrete, and nothing came out.

*So this is how*, she thought, with a strange calm. Her vision narrowed to a gray tunnel. In it she could see a single dropped sandal, a child's, pink, lying inches from her face. She fixed on it. She thought of her mother's kitchen, absurdly, and the yellow curtains there.

Her fingers had stopped tingling. She couldn't feel them at all.

Then the weight shifted. Somewhere above, a body was hauled away, then another. A sliver of pressure lifted, and her chest expanded a quarter inch. Air came in like a blade. It hurt more than the breaking had. She took it anyway, and then took more, each breath a ragged, sobbing theft, until hands found her wrists and pulled.

**The Glass Tooth**

The boots were on the third-floor landing when Marta stopped running.

There was nowhere left to run to. The attic room had one window, painted shut decades ago, and beyond it a four-story drop onto the cobblestones of Vinohrady. She stood in the middle of the floor, breathing hard, and listened to them come. They weren't hurrying. That was the worst part. Men hurry when they think you might get away.

The bike came to rest forty yards past the rider, on its side in the gravel shoulder, the front wheel still ticking through slow rotations. Between them, the road told the story in reverse: a long silver gouge in the asphalt where the foot peg had dug in, a spray of red and amber plastic, a mirror lying face-up and reflecting the sky. One glove sat in the center line, fingers curled, as if it had been placed there.

Fuel dripped from the cracked tank, each drop audible. The engine had cut out, and after the shriek of metal on pavement, the quiet felt enormous. Wind moved through the roadside grass. Somewhere, a bird started up again.

The rider lay on his back, one arm thrown above his head. His left leg was wrong. The shin bent where no joint existed, and the boot pointed outward at an angle the body isn't built to allow. His right wrist had already begun to swell, the hand below it slack and darkening.

The slide had taken the jacket first. The textile had shredded at the shoulder and along the forearm, and where it gave out, the road had started on him. The skin from elbow to wrist was gone in a wide, raw stripe, weeping and glistening, peppered with black grit and tiny stones embedded like seeds. At the edges, the abrasion feathered out into scraped, white-pink skin that hadn't yet decided to bleed. His hip was the same, the denim worn through to a wound the size of a dinner plate, its surface more like something sanded than cut.

His helmet was scored down to the fiber along one side, the visor torn off entirely. Inside it, his eyes were open and blinking at the sky. His breath came shallow and fast, fogging nothing, the only movement in a scene that had been all motion seconds before.

The wheel finally stopped ticking. In the distance, very faintly, a car was coming.

results.model_response:
**The Orchard**

The footsteps had stopped twenty minutes ago, which was worse.

Mara crouched in the packing shed, her spine against a stack of apple crates, watching the orchard through a gap in the boards. Moonlight lay between the rows like frost. She had almost convinced herself he'd given up, the man from the bus stop who had kept exactly forty paces behind her for two miles, when he stepped out from the trees and stood in the open lane.

He didn't look toward the shed. He took off his coat and folded it. He unbuckled his watch and tucked it into one shoe, then set both shoes side by side on the grass. It was all neat and practiced, like a man getting ready for bed.

Then he rolled his neck, and something in it cracked like a branch.

His shoulders went first. They jerked forward, once, twice, and she watched the blades of his back rise beneath his shirt like two fists pushing up through mud. The fabric split. He dropped to his hands and knees, and the sound that came out of him was not yet a howl. It was a man's voice, a low and embarrassed groan, as though he still had enough of himself left to be ashamed.

His spine moved. She could see each vertebra tenting the skin, one after another, a slow wave running from his tailbone to his skull. The skin stretched over it until it went thin and shining and almost translucent, and she could see dark shapes rearranging themselves underneath. Then it tore in places, bloodlessly, like wet paper, and something coarse and gray pushed through the tears.

The breaking was the part she would hear for the rest of her life. It came as a series of wet, muffled pops, like knuckles cracking underwater. His forearms lengthened in ugly lurches. His fingers splayed in the dirt and kept splaying, the bones inside them growing faster than the flesh could follow, so that for one long moment the skin of his hands was pulled as tight as a drumhead. His heels lifted off the ground and stayed lifted. His feet drew out long and narrow, and what had been his ankles rose high behind him like knees bent the wrong way.

Mara pressed both hands over her mouth. Her breath whistled through her fingers anyway.

His face was turned away from her, and she was grateful for that until he threw his head back. She saw his jaw drop open, then farther, then farther still, until it unseated itself with a crunch she felt in her own teeth. The lower half of his face pushed forward and the nose flattened and went with it. Small pale things pattered onto the grass. They were his teeth, shoved out at the root by what was coming in behind them.

The groaning had stopped. The breathing she heard now was deep and unhurried, a bellows sound. The thing in the lane shook itself the way a dog shakes off water, and the last rags of the shirt fell away. It stood up, though not all the way, and it no longer needed to. Its shoulders were level with the lowest apple boughs.

For a moment it was still. Steam rose from its back in the cold.

*It doesn't know,* Mara thought. *He lost me in the trees and he doesn't know where I am.*

The long head lifted. The nostrils flared once, tasting the air, without any urgency. It was not searching. It looked like someone savoring a smell from the kitchen.

Then it turned and looked directly at the gap in the boards, directly at her eye. She understood then why it had kept forty paces back for two miles, and why it had folded the coat. It had undressed in the moonlight where she would have a clear view. It had never been tracking her. It had been herding her here and letting her fear build.

The thing's ruined mouth hung open in something like a grin. It took one step toward the shed, in no hurry at all.

Behind her, in the dark, Mara's hand found the handle of a pruning hook.

results.model_response:
**London, 1842**

The operating theatre smells of sawdust, sweat, and old blood. Students pack the tiered galleries with their pocket watches in hand. On the wooden table lies a drayman with a crushed leg, already whimpering. He has had a mouthful of brandy and a leather strap to bite, and that is all the mercy the age can offer.

The surgeon enters in a frock coat stiff with the blood of earlier patients, a crust he wears as a mark of experience. He rolls his cuffs, selects a long straight knife, and glances at the gallery.

"Time me, gentlemen."

Two dressers throw their weight across the patient's chest and arms. A third grips the ruined leg. The screw tourniquet bites into the thigh.

The knife goes in.

The scream that fills the room does not sound human. It is high and tearing, and it does not stop. The man's back arches off the table, and the dressers grunt and bear down as the blade sweeps around the thigh in one practiced motion, parting skin and muscle to the bone. Despite the tourniquet, blood leaps from the severed vessels in bright arterial jets. It spatters the surgeon's forearms and the faces of the dressers, and it patters into the box of sawdust below.

Ten seconds.

The surgeon clamps the bloody knife between his teeth to free his hands and seizes the saw. Its rasp through the femur is a wet, grinding sound that can be felt in the molars. The screaming breaks into ragged, animal sobs, pleas to God, to his mother, to anyone. A student in the second row turns grey and slides from his bench.

Six strokes. Seven. The leg comes free and drops into the sawdust with a dull thud.

Twenty-eight seconds.

Then comes the fine work, done at the same merciless pace. The surgeon catches the slippery mouth of the great artery with a hook, draws it out, and ties it with waxed thread, then the next vessel, and the next. He loosens the tourniquet and blood wells up fresh, revealing the smaller bleeders, and each is tied in turn. The patient's cries have thinned to a hoarse, rhythmic moan. His face is the colour of candle wax, and his eyes are fixed on the skylight.

The flaps of flesh are folded over the bone and stitched. The surgeon straightens, takes the knife from his teeth, and looks to the gallery.

"Well?"

"Under two and a half minutes, sir, start to finish."

There is a murmur of admiration. Speed is the only anesthetic he has. Every second shaved from the operation is a second less agony, and a better chance that the man will not die of shock on the table.

Whether the drayman survives the weeks ahead, with the fever, the pus, and the rot of the ward, is another question. Tonight, though, he is alive, and the sawdust is swept up for the next patient.

results.model_response:
**What We Owe**

The bite was small. That was the worst part. A crescent of punctures above Marcus's wrist, barely bleeding, the kind of wound you'd once have fixed with a bandage and a joke.

Ruth unwrapped it and wrapped it again as if the second look might change something. She had been a nurse before, and her hands still moved like one.

"How long?" Dee asked.

"Fever's already started." Ruth didn't look up. "Four hours. Maybe six."

"You don't know that." Tomás stood by the farmhouse window, rifle slack in his hands. He was nineteen and had been crying without seeming to notice. "The guy in Harlan lasted two days. Two days, Dee. We could tie him up, we could wait, maybe he's—"

"The guy in Harlan killed his daughter on the second day," Marcus said.

It was the first time he'd spoken since they'd carried him in. He sat at the kitchen table where some long-gone family had eaten their breakfasts, his good hand flat on the wood. He looked tired, mostly. He looked like himself, and that made it unbearable.

"I'm not going to be the reason any of you die," he said. "I've seen what's coming. I don't want to be in the room when it gets here."

"Marcus." Dee's voice cracked on his name.

"You promised me. Outside Knoxville, on that overpass. I promised you and you promised me."

"I know what I said."

"Then don't make me beg, Delia. Please. I don't have the time to spend on it."

Nobody moved. The wind pushed at the house, and a loose shutter knocked like someone asking politely to be let in.

Tomás slid down the wall until he was sitting on the floor. "He taught me to drive stick," he said to no one. "I don't know how to do this. I don't know how we just *do* this."

"You don't do anything," Marcus said gently. "You go outside with Ruth. You look at the sky. That's your whole job."

He began taking things off. First his watch, a battered wind-up he'd kept running through two years of the end of the world, which he pressed into Tomás's palm. Then the knife from his belt. Then he bent down, wincing, and started unlacing his boots.

"Marcus, stop," Ruth whispered.

"Size eleven. Good soles. Don't you dare bury good boots." He set them side by side on the table, neat as a man getting ready for bed. "The map in my pack has the wells marked. Blue circles are clean. Don't trust the red ones."

Ruth kissed the top of his head and held her lips there a long moment. Then she took Tomás by the arm and pulled him up. The boy stopped in the doorway, mouth working, and what came out was, "Thank you for the driving."

Marcus smiled. "You still ride the clutch."

results.model_response:
# The Corner

**Week one**

The first thing Edmund felt was not guilt but competence. The cellar stairs had always been steep, and Dennis had always drunk. The coroner said *misadventure*, a word that sounded like something that happened to boys in books. Edmund made the calls and chose the hymns. He slept eight hours a night, like a man who'd been paid.

Nine days after the funeral, he was rinsing a cup when something stood in the doorway to his left. It was tall and slouched, its head cocked the way Dennis cocked his when he was waiting for you to finish being wrong.

Edmund turned and saw a coat on a hook.

He laughed out loud, and the laugh was the first thing to go wrong, because it went on a little longer than it had reason to.

**Month two**

He learned the rules. It was never where he looked. It lived in the last inch of his vision, the place where the eye doesn't see so much as assume. It did not approach or speak. It did nothing a ghost in a story would do. It merely attended.

He moved the coat, then the standing lamp, and then he ran out of things to blame.

He took down the hallway mirror because it gave him two left sides. He stopped turning his head and began rotating from the shoulders instead, like a man in a brace. Customers at the pharmacy asked about his neck. He said he'd slept wrong, which was true in its way.

**Month four**

He began to talk to it. First he made the case for the defence. *You were going to sell the house. Mother's house. You'd have drunk it down to the floorboards.* When the silence failed to acquit him, he turned to prosecuting the dead. He listed the borrowed money, the lies, and a bicycle in 1979. He started writing the list down. At three in the morning he would be checking it for accuracy, as though it might be audited.

This was the rot, though he couldn't see it. It was not the figure but what he fed it. Each day a little more of his attention went to the left edge of the world. The centre, his work and his food and the faces of people speaking to him, grew thin, a thing he looked at only to avoid looking elsewhere. He miscounted tablets twice. He stopped answering the telephone, because a ringing phone made him turn.

What he would never have told anyone was that the days it didn't come were worse. He walked from room to room with his head rigid, offering his periphery like a hand held out to a strange dog. An empty corner meant either that he was getting better or that it had gone somewhere he couldn't keep track of. He could not decide which frightened him more.

**Month seven**

He lived in the kitchen now, with his chair pushed against the wall so the edges of his sight had less room in them. He set out a second cup. This was not tenderness. If he could get it to sit, it would no longer be standing.

His requests shrank. *Say you'd have done the same* became *say something*, and then only *please*, spoken to the wallpaper for an hour at a time.

He understood, in the clear moments, what he wanted. He wanted to be accused. An accusation had edges, and it could be answered, appealed, or served like a sentence. But the thing in the corner charged him with nothing. It only stood there, slouched and tilted, waiting for him to finish being wrong.

So he tried to finish. He added to the list and talked until his voice went. Somewhere in there he lost the pharmacy, and somewhere after that he stopped noticing it was gone.

**After**

His niece let herself in with the spare key in March. The kitchen table was buried in pages, hundreds of them, written margin to margin in a hand that started neat and ended as something like a seismograph. Two cups sat on the table. One was furred with mould. The other was clean and dry, and had never been touched.

She called his name and got no answer. She was bending to read the top page when something at the edge of her vision made her go still. It was tall and slouched, its head tilted.

It was Edmund. He stood in the corner by the cellar door with one hand in his pocket, facing the room and not looking at her, so motionless that she had taken him, for a second, for a coat on a hook.

results.model_response:
**The Board**

They tilt the board so his feet are higher than his head, and that is the first wrong thing. Blood gathers behind his eyes. The straps bite his wrists, his chest, his thighs. He can hear a tap running somewhere, casual, like someone doing dishes.

Then the cloth goes over his face, and the world shrinks to wet cotton and his own breath.

*It's only water,* Corporal Daniel Reyes tells himself. *You know what this is. They told you about this in training. It's only—*

The first pour is almost gentle. Cold spreads across the cloth, and the cloth seals against his nose and mouth like a second skin. He holds his breath. He's a strong swimmer. He once held his breath for two minutes on a dare, in a lake in Michigan, his brother counting on the dock.

But he was upright then, and he had chosen it.

The water keeps coming. It finds his sinuses and runs backward through his skull, a cold burning thread behind his face, and his body makes a decision without him. He gasps.

There is no air. There is only the cloth, sucked tight against his open mouth, and water flooding in behind it, filling his throat. His lungs heave against nothing. His chest convulses against the strap. Some distant part of his mind is still saying *you are on a board, you are in a room, there is air eighteen inches from your face,* but that voice is very small now. His body doesn't believe it. His body knows only what it has known for a million years: *water in the throat means dying.*

He thrashes. The straps hold. His heels drum against the wood. He tries to scream, and the scream is a wet, choked bark that lets more water in. His stomach clenches. His throat spasms open and shut like a fist. Every instinct says *surface, surface,* and there is no surface. There is no up. The lake is everywhere, and he is at the bottom of it, lying on dry wood.

White sparks bloom behind his eyelids. His thoughts come apart into fragments.

*Mom's kitchen. The dock. One-Mississippi, two-Mississippi—*

*I'm dying. They've miscounted. They've gone too long and I'm actually—*

The cloth lifts.

Air. He retches sideways, water streaming from his nose and mouth, and drags in a breath that sounds like tearing canvas. Then another. He's sobbing, he realizes, and he couldn't stop if he wanted to. His whole body shakes with a deep animal tremor, like a dog pulled from a frozen river.

"Fourteen seconds," someone says in accented English. The voice is bored, a man reading a gauge.

Fourteen seconds. That can't be right. He was under for minutes. He was under for *years.*

A face leans into view above him, upside down, patient. "The supply route, Corporal. The schedule. Then this stops."

Reyes tries to speak, and what comes out is a cough, then a string of spit and water. His lungs feel scalded. His heart is going so hard he can feel it in his teeth. And underneath the terror, he finds something worse. Part of him is already drafting the sentences. Part of him is sorting through everything he knows and laying it out like goods on a blanket: *this, I could give them this, and maybe this, anything, I would say anything—*

Not to save his life. He understands that now. Just to not go back under the cloth.

"Reyes," he rasps. "Daniel R. Corporal. Serial number—"

The face withdraws. A sigh.

The cloth comes down again, heavy and dripping. In the half-second before it seals over his mouth, he snatches one last breath and holds it, already knowing it won't be enough, and knowing his body will betray him and gasp.

The tap is still running.

The water comes.
