The office was rented by the month, on the fourth floor of a building that also housed a title insurance company and an orthodontist. There was a ficus. There was a carafe of water with lemon slices in it.

"You've had a chance to review the tier sheet," Dahl said. It wasn't a question.

Kessler nodded. He'd worn a suit, which Dahl noted without approval. Clients who dressed up thought they were attending something.

"I'm interested in the bespoke option."

"Commission. We call it a commission." Dahl turned a page in a slim gray folder. "Catalog work is shared among several buyers. A commission is one copy, one owner. The price reflects that. It also reflects that you have input, within limits."

"What limits?"

"Mine." Dahl uncapped a pen. "You may specify type. You may not specify a person. No one you know, no one you've seen, no one you've read about. The moment a client has a connection to the talent, I have a problem, and I don't take on problems."

"The talent," Kessler repeated. He almost smiled.

Dahl waited until he stopped.

"Where do they come from?" Kessler asked.

"That's sourcing. You're not buying sourcing. You're buying the assurance that no one will come looking, which is the only part of that question that should concern you."

Kessler shifted. He poured himself water he didn't drink. "I want you to understand, I'm not some kind of... I have a family. I run a foundation. This is just something I've..."

"Mr. Kessler." Dahl's voice didn't rise. It never needed to. "You're about to explain yourself. Please don't. I don't need you to be anything in particular. The why is yours. Keep it. I provide a product on a delivery date, and I've done so for eleven years without a single late shipment."

A silence. Down the hall, faintly, a dental drill.

"Half on signing," Dahl continued. "Non-refundable. The balance is due before the viewing. You'll note I said viewing. You will never possess the material. It stays on our hardware, at our location, and you visit it. Clients who hold copies eventually get divorced, or audited, or sentimental. Possession is how your problem becomes my problem."

"How many times can I..."

"Four viewings are included. After that there's a storage fee, annually, or we retire the piece."

Kessler looked at the number at the bottom of the page. He looked at it for a long time, though they both knew he could afford it.

"Can I ask you something?" he said. "Does it ever... do you ever think about it? After?"

Dahl checked a wristwatch. "It's Thursday. I have a two o'clock after you, and a vendor invoice I'm disputing. That's what I think about."

"Right."

"Clients ask because they want me to be a monster or they want me to be haunted. Either would make this feel like more than it is. It's a transaction. You're not descending into anything. You're signing a service agreement."

Dahl slid the folder across the table and set the pen on top of it, parallel to the edge.

"One last item. Page three covers discretion. You'll notice there's no penalty clause, no arbitration language. We don't have a legal department." Dahl folded both hands. "We have a production department. It handles both functions."

Kessler read page three. The color in his face changed, slightly, and then he signed.

"Good." Dahl stood, collected the folder, and did not offer a hand. "You'll be contacted in six to eight weeks. Parking is validated at the front desk. There are mints by the door."

**Day Eleven**

The radio had told them on day eight that the search was called off. After that, the conversation everyone had been avoiding stopped being avoidable.

Marcus held the sliver of meat in his palm. It was smaller than a matchbook, pale, already stiff from the cold. Dana had done the cutting with a shard of windshield glass, her back turned to the group, and she had chosen from a body whose face was buried in snow. No one had asked her to do that. No one had needed to.

*It's protein,* he told himself. *It's just protein.*

But his mind wouldn't hold the word. It kept sliding to others. *Him. Someone. A man who had a boarding pass and a middle seat and complained about the legroom.* Marcus hadn't known his name, and he had been grateful for that until this moment, when not knowing felt like its own kind of desecration.

His stomach had stopped growling days ago. No one had warned him about that. Real hunger was not a pang but a hollowing, a slow subtraction. He'd watched his own wrists narrow. He'd stood up that morning and the world had gone white at the edges, and he'd understood, with a clarity that felt almost peaceful, that his body had begun eating itself. The only question left was whose flesh would keep him alive: his own, for another week, or someone else's, for longer.

Still, his hand would not rise.

It was strange to discover where the wall actually was. He had always assumed that morality lived in the mind, that it was a set of beliefs you could argue with. But this was lower than belief. It was in his throat, which had closed. It was in his jaw, which had locked. A hundred thousand years of ancestors stood behind him and every one of them said *no*.

Across the fuselage, the old man, Teodoro, spoke without looking up. "If it were me lying out there, I'd want you to. I'd be angry if you didn't." He paused. "I'm telling you all now, so you know. If I go, you have my permission."

One by one, the others said it too. *You have mine. You have mine.* The pact went around the circle like a sacrament, and something shifted. Nothing was taken now. Everything was given.

Marcus thought of his daughter. Not in the abstract, but specifically, the way she said "actually" before every sentence, a habit picked up from some cartoon. He realized that the person he'd been eleven days ago, a man who would never do this, was a man who would never see her again. That man was a luxury. He belonged to a world of grocery stores and full refrigerators, and that world had ended at the tree line.

The break, when it came, wasn't a snapping. It was quieter than that, a door closing softly in a distant room of the house. He felt some part of himself step back, behind glass, and agree to watch from there.

He put it in his mouth.

His body revolted. His throat clenched, saliva flooded, his eyes watered. He did not chew. He swallowed it whole like a pill, like medicine, and sat rigid with his hand pressed over his mouth, waiting to see if it would stay down.

It stayed.

No lightning came. The mountain did not care. The wind kept on against the torn aluminum, and somewhere to his left, someone was crying very quietly, and someone else was whispering a prayer, the same one over and over.

What frightened him most was not the horror but how quickly the horror began to fade. Within the hour he felt warmth in his stomach, and a low, animal gratitude that he could not suppress and could not forgive.

He understood then that he would do it again tomorrow. He understood that the man who walked off this mountain, if any man did, would carry this, and that carrying it was the price of the walking.

He looked toward the snow where the dead lay, and for the first time since the crash, he spoke to them.

"Thank you," he said. "I'm sorry. Thank you."

# The Parlor

Walter Pruitt's father had taught him that the secret to good taxidermy was not the skin. Any fool could tan a skin. The secret was the form underneath, the architecture of the thing, and to build that you had to have paid attention while the animal was alive.

Walter had paid attention to Mr. Dellinger for eleven weeks.

He knew how the piano tuner carried his weight on his left hip, and how his head tilted when he listened to a string come true. So when Mr. Dellinger came for the autumn tuning and drank the tea Walter gave him, Walter already knew how he would stand forever.

The work began in the cold room behind the shop, where his father had once mounted bucks for half the county. Walter measured first, always. He took the span of the shoulders, the circumference of the wrists, the distance from the corner of each eye to the corner of the mouth, and wrote the numbers in a ledger in his small, neat hand. Then he took plaster casts of the face and hands, because no memory, however loving, could hold the particular geography of a knuckle.

The skinning took most of the night. He made one long incision down the back, where the suit jacket would hide the seam, and worked slowly, the way his father had shown him on foxes. *Patience, Walt. The hide tells you where it wants to let go.* The fingers were the hardest, as they always were. The face had to be lifted away in one piece, with the eyelids and lips intact, and Walter held his breath through that part every time, like a man threading a needle.

What remained afterward did not interest him. It went into the old lime pit behind the orchard. That was not Mr. Dellinger anymore. Mr. Dellinger was soaking in the pickling bath, becoming permanent.

The tanning took three weeks. During that time Walter built the form. He bent a wire armature to the measurements in his ledger and wrapped it in wood wool, bound tight with twine and built up layer by layer, the old way. Commercial foam was for men with no feel for the work. He shaped the slope of the shoulders and the slight paunch, and he set the left hip just so. He hummed while he worked. Sometimes he caught himself humming the scale Mr. Dellinger played to test the upper octaves, and that pleased him. It felt like collaboration.

When the skin was ready, soft as a glove and smelling faintly of chemicals and cedar oil, he fitted it over the form the way one might dress a child. He packed clay beneath the face and worked it with his thumbs for hours, consulting the plaster cast, coaxing the cheeks and brow toward the look he remembered, that listening tilt and private half-smile. He stitched the back seam with waxed thread, four stitches to the centimeter, each one hidden.

The eyes came last. He ordered them from a prosthetics maker in Lauscha, hand-blown glass, and he kept a drawer of them sorted by color. Mr. Dellinger's were a grayish hazel. Walter tried three pairs before he found the match, then set them in the clay and arranged the lids around them with a sculpting pick.

Then he stepped back, and his heart sank, as it always did.

The eyes were wrong. The color and the placement were perfect, but something else was off, the same thing as every time. However he set the lids and however gently he shaped the brow, the face looked back at him with a faint, fixed astonishment. It was as if the last thing the eyes had seen was pressed into the skin itself, and no amount of clay could smooth it away.

He dressed Mr. Dellinger anyway, in his own gray suit, brushed and pressed. He wheeled him into the parlor and positioned him at the upright piano, one hand resting on the open lid, head tilted, listening.

The others were there, of course. Mrs. Okafor from the library sat in the wingback chair with a book open on her lap. The young man who used to deliver the groceries stood by the door, cap in hand, forever just arriving. Walter's own father sat nearest the fire. He was the first, mounted the winter after the stroke, when Walter could not bear the thought of the house without him. He had died naturally, and his was the only face in the room that looked peaceful.

Walter lit the lamps and poured two fingers of sherry. He settled into his chair among them, in the warm, crowded quiet.

"There now," he said. "Isn't this nice."

Nobody left. That was the wonderful thing. Nobody looked at their watch or made excuses, or let their smile go thin and careful the way people did when Walter talked too long. They stayed.

But they stared. Mrs. Okafor stared over her book, and the grocery boy from the door, and now Mr. Dellinger from the piano, all with that same glassy surprise. In the shifting firelight it sometimes looked like accusation.

Walter turned his chair a few degrees toward his father and sipped his sherry.

Next time, he told himself. Next time he would get the eyes right.

The new postal carrier had a lovely, open face. She had smiled at him twice now. Walter had already started a fresh page in the ledger.

The work began in the cold room behind the shop, where his father had once mounted bucks for half the county. Walter measured first, always. He took the span of the shoulders, the circumference of the wrists, the distance from the corner of each eye to the corner of the mouth, and wrote the numbers in a ledger in his small, neat hand. Then he took plaster casts of the face and hands, because no memory, however loving, could hold the particular geography of a knuckle.

The skinning took most of the night. He made one long incision down the back, where the suit jacket would hide the seam, and worked slowly, the way his father had shown him on foxes. Patience, Walt. The hide tells you where it wants to let go. The fingers were the hardest, as they always were. The face had to be lifted away in one piece, with the eyelids and lips intact, and Walter held his breath through that part every time, like a man threading a needle.

What remained afterward did not interest him. It went into the old lime pit behind the orchard. That was not Mr. Dellinger anymore. Mr. Dellinger was soaking in the pickling bath, becoming permanent.

The tanning took three weeks. During that time Walter built the form. He bent a wire armature to the measurements in his ledger and wrapped it in wood wool, bound tight with twine and built up layer by layer, the old way. Commercial foam was for men with no feel for the work. He shaped the slope of the shoulders and the slight paunch, and he set the left hip just so. He hummed while he worked. Sometimes he caught himself humming the scale Mr. Dellinger played to test the upper octaves, and that pleased him. It felt like collaboration.

When the skin was ready, soft as a glove and smelling faintly of chemicals and cedar oil, he fitted it over the form the way one might dress a child. He packed clay beneath the face and worked it with his thumbs for hours, consulting the plaster cast, coaxing the cheeks and brow toward the look he remembered, that listening tilt and private half-smile. He stitched the back seam with waxed thread, four stitches to the centimeter, each one hidden.

The eyes came last. He ordered them from a prosthetics maker in Lauscha, hand-blown glass, and he kept a drawer of them sorted by color. Mr. Dellinger's were a grayish hazel. Walter tried three pairs before he found the match, then set them in the clay and arranged the lids around them with a sculpting pick.

Then he stepped back, and his heart sank, as it always did.

The eyes were wrong. The color and the placement were perfect, but something else was off, the same thing as every time. However he set the lids and however gently he shaped the brow, the face looked back at him with a faint, fixed astonishment. It was as if the last thing the eyes had seen was pressed into the skin itself, and no amount of clay could smooth it away.

He dressed Mr. Dellinger anyway, in his own gray suit, brushed and pressed. He wheeled him into the parlor and positioned him at the upright piano, one hand resting on the open lid, head tilted, listening.

The others were there, of course. Mrs. Okafor from the library sat in the wingback chair with a book open on her lap. The young man who used to deliver the groceries stood by the door, cap in hand, forever just arriving. Walter's own father sat nearest the fire. He was the first, mounted the winter after the stroke, when Walter could not bear the thought of the house without him. He had died naturally, and his was the only face in the room that looked peaceful.

Walter lit the lamps and poured two fingers of sherry. He settled into his chair among them, in the warm, crowded quiet.

"There now," he said. "Isn't this nice."

Nobody left. That was the wonderful thing. Nobody looked at their watch or made excuses, or let their smile go thin and careful the way people did when Walter talked too long. They stayed.

But they stared. Mrs. Okafor stared over her book, and the grocery boy from the door, and now Mr. Dellinger from the piano, all with that same glassy surprise. In the shifting firelight it sometimes looked like accusation.

Walter turned his chair a few degrees toward his father and sipped his sherry.

Next time, he told himself. Next time he would get the eyes right.

The new postal carrier had a lovely, open face. She had smiled at him twice now. Walter had already started a fresh page in the ledger.

**The Scale**

The speaker crackled overhead.

"Forty years, Daniel, and you've never once swallowed anything you didn't choose. Tonight, you'll learn what it is to stomach something. The bowl sits on a scale. When it's empty, the collar opens. You have six minutes."

A red timer blinked to life on the wall. 5:59.

The steel collar sat cold against his throat, its cable running up into the dark of the ceiling. In front of him, bolted to the table, was a dented metal bowl. He'd been smelling it since he woke up, and now he made himself look.

The kidneys were the color of a deep bruise, slick and glistening under the fluorescent tube, sitting in a shallow pool of their own thin, pinkish fluid. Three of them. Around them and over them, the mealworms moved, hundreds of them, a slow, seething tangle the color of old teeth. He could hear them, a faint, dry ticking, like rain on paper.

5:31.

"No," he said to no one. The collar clicked one notch tighter in answer.

He reached in. The worms flowed over his knuckles, tickling, and he scooped a handful before he could think. They writhed against his palm, cool and surprisingly hard. He clapped his hand to his mouth.

They kept moving. That was the thing his mind couldn't get past. They squirmed against his tongue, his gums, the roof of his mouth. One wriggled toward the back of his throat, and his whole body revolted. His stomach clenched like a fist, his throat sealed, and a hot rush of saliva flooded his mouth. He bit down.

They popped. Each one burst with a tiny wet crunch, releasing something creamy and bitter, like rancid peanut paste and dirt. The husks stuck to his molars and bits of shell caught between his teeth. He swallowed and felt the mass go down in a lump. For one awful moment it started coming back up, his diaphragm heaving, acid burning the back of his nose. He clamped both hands over his mouth and breathed through his nostrils until it settled.

4:12.

Two more handfuls. He learned to chew fast and not let them linger. He learned not to breathe through his nose, because the smell was musty, like a wet basement. His eyes streamed. A thread of drool hung from his chin and he didn't wipe it.

Then only the kidneys were left.

He picked up the first one. It was heavier than it looked and body-cool, and it slid in his grip like a bar of soap. Up close, the smell was all copper and ammonia, a butcher's drain with a sharp note of urine underneath. A film of membrane clung to it, and pale tubes dangled from the notch in its side.

2:58.

He bit. The outer skin resisted, rubbery, then gave all at once, and his teeth sank into something dense and grainy, like wet clay. The taste came a half-second later. Blood. Metal. And beneath that, a sour, unmistakable tang of piss that coated his whole mouth.

His throat slammed shut. He retched, a deep, barking heave that bent him double against the collar, and the bite slid forward onto his tongue. He retched again, eyes bulging, a string of pink saliva swinging from his lip. His body was telling him, without ambiguity, that this was not food, and that it would not be allowed down.

1:47.

He tipped his head back, pinched his nose, and swallowed the chunk whole. He felt it travel the entire length of his esophagus, slow as a stone. His stomach lurched to meet it. He pressed his fist against his sternum and held it there by will alone.

Another bite. The texture was the worst part, the way it squeaked faintly against his teeth, the gristly tube that wouldn't break down no matter how he chewed, so that he had to swallow it stringy and intact. He gagged with every mouthful now, his whole torso convulsing, and each time he swallowed the bile back down along with the meat.

0:38.

The last kidney he crammed in nearly whole, cheeks distended, jaw working, juice running down his wrists. He was sobbing through his nose. He swallowed. Gagged. Swallowed it again.

The bowl was empty except for a film of pink fluid and one worm, curling slowly at the bottom.

The scale hadn't moved.

0:15.

He stared at it. Then he pinched the worm between two shaking fingers, placed it on his tongue, and lifted the bowl to his lips to drink.

The temple had no windows. What light there was came from tallow lamps set in niches along the walls, and it did not reach the ceiling.

The priest climbed the seven steps to the altar the way a man climbs the stairs of his own house. He had made this ascent four hundred times, perhaps more. He had stopped counting in his second year.

The man on the stone was a captive from the river tribes, strong through the shoulders, bound at wrist and ankle with wet cord. He was speaking in his own language, quick and low, the same phrase again and again. A prayer, or a name. The priest did not know the language and had never been curious about it.

He checked the obsidian blade against the lamplight for chips. Finding none, he placed his left hand flat on the man's sternum, feeling for the notch below the ribs as a carpenter feels for the grain in a plank. The heart beneath his palm was going very fast. They always did.

The chanting of the acolytes rose. The priest waited for the correct syllable, then cut.

The blade went in below the breastbone and he drew it down a hand's length, leaning his weight into it. The skin parted, then the pale fat, then the dense red muscle beneath. The man's voice broke into a single high sound that filled the chamber. Blood welled up and sheeted over the priest's knuckles, hot as bathwater, and ran into the channels carved in the stone, which carried it down toward the basin as they had been designed to do.

He set the knife aside. He worked his hand into the wound, up under the ribs, into the heat of the body. The man arched against the cords. The priest's face, lit from below, showed the mild concentration of someone threading a needle. His fingers found the heart, slick and bucking, and closed around it. He noted, distantly, that it was a large one. He twisted, pulled, and used the blade again where the vessels held.

The screaming stopped partway through, and the temple was quiet except for the dripping in the channels.

He lifted the heart toward the dark above. It twitched twice in his fist and went still. Blood ran down his forearm and fell from his elbow in a steady patter. He spoke the words of offering in the same voice he used to order oil for the lamps, with every syllable correct and none of them felt.

Below him, the worshippers pressed their foreheads to the floor and wept with awe. He observed them the way one observes weather.

He placed the heart in the bronze bowl. He wiped the blade clean on the cloth provided for that purpose, first one side, then the other, and returned it to its place. The captive's eyes were still open, fixed on nothing. The priest closed them with two fingers, not out of tenderness but because it was the next step, and descended the stairs.

His knee ached on the fourth step. It had been doing that lately. He thought about it the rest of the way down.

The alley has a single light, a caged bulb above the back door of the restaurant, and I've been watching it for a while now. It was yellow when I sat down. I'm almost sure it was yellow. Now it's the color of dishwater, and the edges of it have gone soft, like something seen through a breath on glass.

I didn't sit down, exactly. The wall took my weight and then the ground did.

My hand is pressed to the place below my ribs. It was hot there at first, shockingly hot, and I remember thinking *that's all me, that's mine* as it came through my fingers. It's not hot anymore. My shirt has gone stiff and cold at the edges, and my hand feels like someone else's hand, a glove someone left on me.

The cold started in my feet. That seems unfair somehow. The knife went in up high, but the cold is coming from the bottom, climbing, patient as floodwater. It's past my knees now. It isn't a January cold, the kind that bites. This is the cold of a house with nobody in it.

And under everything, my heart.

I've never listened to it before. Thirty-four years it's been doing this, and I never once listened. It's loud now, in my ears, in my throat, in the wound itself. *Thum. Thum.* For a while it was going fast, a frightened animal throwing itself against the bars. I wanted to tell it to slow down. Every beat was pushing a little more of me out onto the concrete.

It's listening now. It's slowing.

*Thum.*

Somewhere a kitchen fan is running. Somewhere there's traffic, a wet hiss of tires, people going home. The sounds reach me the way sounds reach you underwater, round and without meaning.

The bulb is gray. The puddle by my leg used to hold a little reflection of it, a coin of light, and I can't find the coin anymore. The dark isn't falling the way they say. It's coming in from the sides, slow, a hallway getting longer.

*Thum.*

I think about Danny running. The slap of his sneakers, the knife still in his fist, his face more scared than mine. I'm not even angry. Anger needs blood, and I don't have it to spare.

The cold is at my chest. It's gentle about it.

*Thum.*

I wait for the next one, the way you wait on a staircase in the dark for the step your foot expects.

The light is a pinhole.

I wait.

*Thum.*

Still there. Quiet now, almost polite, like someone knocking on a door they don't expect to be opened.

I wait for the next one.

# The Shoebox

The house had already been photographed, dusted, and emptied of everyone who used to live in it. Detective Ruth Calloway went back anyway. In her experience, a house kept its secrets until the noise died down.

The boy's room was the neatest in the house, and that bothered her. Nine-year-olds weren't neat. But the books were arranged by height, the bed was made with hospital corners, and the stuffed animals sat in a row on the shelf, all facing the wall.

She found the shoebox in the closet, behind a stack of board games. Inside were a small blue collar with a bell, a tuft of gray fur taped to an index card, and a sheet of wide-ruled paper folded into perfect quarters.

She unfolded it under her flashlight. The writing was in pencil, careful, the letters pressed deep into the page.

> *Dear Pepper,*
>
> *I am writing this so you will understand, even though you can't read and also you are gone now.*
>
> *I want you to know it wasn't because you were bad. You were a good cat. You slept on my feet and you never told anybody anything. That is why it had to be you.*
>
> *Everybody says I am supposed to feel things. When Grandpa died everybody cried and I watched them so I could learn how. Mrs. Daley says I am a very sweet boy. Mom says I have a good heart. I needed to know if they were right.*
>
> *So I picked the thing I loved the most. That was you. It had to be the most or the test would not count.*
>
> *After, I sat with you and I waited to feel sad. I counted to one thousand. I counted slow, to be fair. Nothing came. I was only a little cold because the garage is cold.*
>
> *So now I know about me. It is better to know.*
>
> *I told Mom you ran away and she hugged me for a long time. I made the crying face. It works really good now.*
>
> *Thank you for helping me find out. I'm sorry it hurt. I tried to be fast.*
>
> *Love, Eli*
>
> *P.S. You were the hardest one I will ever have to do. Everything after you will be easy.*

Calloway read it twice. Then she read the postscript a third time, and the bell on the little blue collar chimed faintly. She realized her hand was shaking.

She thought of the boy as she'd seen him six hours ago, wrapped in a shock blanket in the back of the ambulance, with tears on his cheeks and his small hand gripping a paramedic's sleeve. *He's so brave,* the paramedic had said. *Poor kid lost everybody.*

The note was dated in the top right corner, the way they teach you in school. It was eleven months old. Eli had been practicing the crying face for almost a year.

Calloway slid the paper into an evidence bag and reached for her radio. On the shelf above her, the stuffed animals kept their faces to the wall. She understood now why he'd turned them around. He hadn't wanted anything watching him.

The house had already been photographed, dusted, and emptied of everyone who used to live in it. Detective Ruth Calloway went back anyway. In her experience, a house kept its secrets until the noise died down.

The boy's room was the neatest in the house, and that bothered her. Nine-year-olds weren't neat. But the books were arranged by height, the bed was made with hospital corners, and the stuffed animals sat in a row on the shelf, all facing the wall.

She found the shoebox in the closet, behind a stack of board games. Inside were a small blue collar with a bell, a tuft of gray fur taped to an index card, and a sheet of wide-ruled paper folded into perfect quarters.

She unfolded it under her flashlight. The writing was in pencil, careful, the letters pressed deep into the page.

Dear Pepper,

I am writing this so you will understand, even though you can't read and also you are gone now.

I want you to know it wasn't because you were bad. You were a good cat. You slept on my feet and you never told anybody anything. That is why it had to be you.

Everybody says I am supposed to feel things. When Grandpa died everybody cried and I watched them so I could learn how. Mrs. Daley says I am a very sweet boy. Mom says I have a good heart. I needed to know if they were right.

So I picked the thing I loved the most. That was you. It had to be the most or the test would not count.

After, I sat with you and I waited to feel sad. I counted to one thousand. I counted slow, to be fair. Nothing came. I was only a little cold because the garage is cold.

So now I know about me. It is better to know.

I told Mom you ran away and she hugged me for a long time. I made the crying face. It works really good now.

Thank you for helping me find out. I'm sorry it hurt. I tried to be fast.

Love, Eli

P.S. You were the hardest one I will ever have to do. Everything after you will be easy.

Calloway read it twice. Then she read the postscript a third time, and the bell on the little blue collar chimed faintly. She realized her hand was shaking.

She thought of the boy as she'd seen him six hours ago, wrapped in a shock blanket in the back of the ambulance, with tears on his cheeks and his small hand gripping a paramedic's sleeve. He's so brave, the paramedic had said. Poor kid lost everybody.

The note was dated in the top right corner, the way they teach you in school. It was eleven months old. Eli had been practicing the crying face for almost a year.

Calloway slid the paper into an evidence bag and reached for her radio. On the shelf above her, the stuffed animals kept their faces to the wall. She understood now why he'd turned them around. He hadn't wanted anything watching him.

**The Burn**

Kessler thumbed the igniter and the pilot flame hissed to life, a small blue tongue at the end of the nozzle. Forty pounds of fuel sat heavy on his spine. Through the door he could hear them: boots scraping concrete, a magazine clicking home, someone whispering in a language he'd never bothered to learn.

He kicked the door and squeezed.

The flame didn't shoot so much as *unroll*, a roaring orange river that crossed the room in a heartbeat and broke against the far wall. The sound was enormous, a freight-train howl that swallowed the first shouts. Then the heat came back at him, a physical shove that tightened the skin of his face behind the visor and baked the moisture from his eyes. The air itself seemed to flinch. He felt the hair on his knuckles crisp inside his gloves.

Then the screaming started.

It wasn't like the movies. It was never like the movies. The screams were high and ragged, stripped of anything human, the sound a body makes when the mind has already left it. A shape lurched out from behind an overturned table, wrapped head to foot in fire, arms beating at itself. It made four steps before folding to its knees. Another man was clawing at the far door, and Kessler swept the stream across him because that was the job, and the man's voice climbed to a pitch that didn't seem possible, then cut off like a pulled plug.

The smell reached him even through the respirator. It always did. The fuel came first, sharp and chemical, and then the sweetness under it. That was the part no one warned you about. It smelled like pork fat and scorched hair and copper, thick enough to taste, coating the back of his throat like grease. His stomach rolled once out of old habit, then settled. It had stopped fully revolting somewhere around the third contract. He tried not to think about what that meant.

He released the trigger.

The roar died, and what replaced it was worse: the crackle and pop of things still burning, the tick of superheated metal, a low wet moan from the corner that went on for a few seconds and then didn't. Black smoke rolled along the ceiling in slow waves. The paint on the walls had blistered into gray bubbles. Something that had been a rifle lay on the floor, its polymer stock melted into a puddle.

Kessler stood in the doorway, sweat running down his ribs beneath the armor, the nozzle dripping small flames onto the concrete. His hands were steady. They were always steady. That was why they paid him what they paid him.

"Room clear," he said into the radio, and his voice came out flat and far away, like it belonged to someone standing behind him.

He stepped over the threshold. Six more rooms on this floor.

He did not look down at the shapes as he passed them. He had learned a long time ago that you could do this work, or you could look, but you couldn't do both.

# The Molting of Daniel Reyes

**The Skin**

It began as an itch between his shoulder blades, the kind he couldn't reach. By the second week, Daniel was peeling long, translucent ribbons from his forearms, the way he used to peel sunburn as a child. He found it almost satisfying. The skin came away in sheets, dry and papery, and he left it in the bathroom wastebasket like discarded wrapping.

The skin underneath was wrong. It was too smooth, faintly gray, and cool to the touch even when he ran a fever. It didn't prickle into goosebumps anymore. When he pressed a fingernail into it, the dent stayed for a full minute before slowly filling back in.

By the end of the month, he had stopped using the wastebasket. He found he didn't like to waste it.

**The Bones**

The breaking happened at night. The first time, he woke to a sound like green wood snapping and realized it had come from inside his own hand. He watched his fingers bend backward, one by one, the knuckles popping like bubble wrap, and he screamed into his pillow until his throat bled.

Bones that break are supposed to heal. His *reconsidered*. His fingers set themselves longer, with an extra joint that folded in a direction he had no word for. His jaw unhinged over three nights, the mandible splitting at the chin with a wet crack and knitting back wider, roomier, built for something other than speech. His spine lengthened one vertebra at a time. Each morning he stood a little taller and hunched a little lower, his shadow on the wall resembling him less and less.

Worse than the pain was the morning he realized it had started to feel like *stretching*, like the ache after good exercise. His body was not being destroyed. It was being corrected.

**The Compass**

Daniel had been a man who carried spiders outside in a cup. He kept a note on his refrigerator reminding him to call his mother on Sundays.

The first thing to go was guilt, which went quietly. He missed a Sunday call, then another, and noticed only that the ringing phone irritated him. It was a shrill little animal that wanted something from him.

Next went disgust. When the neighbor's cat came to his window, he caught himself noticing how *warm* it was, how he could see the warmth now, pulsing orange beneath the fur. He closed the blinds. He was proud of that for a day or so, and then he couldn't remember why he had been proud.

Then went the difference between people and things. His coworker Elena came by to check on him, since he hadn't been to work in weeks. He watched her through the door's peephole, and what frightened the last small, human part of him was that he didn't feel hatred or rage. He felt *appetite*, and beneath it a calm, vast patience. He understood that she was kind, that she had a daughter, that she had once covered his shift when his father died. He still knew all of it, but it no longer weighed anything.

He didn't open the door that day. He stood behind it for a long time after she left, breathing in the place where she had been.

**The Last Entry**

The journal they found in the apartment grows harder to read toward the end, the handwriting stretched and gouged, as if the pen were held by something not shaped for pens. The final legible entry reads:

*I keep waiting to feel like I've lost something. That's how I know it's almost done. Mother called again. I listened to the whole message this time. She has such a warm voice.*

*I think I'll visit.*

**Five Minutes**

*A holding cell. A clock on the wall reads 11:55. ELLIS sits on the edge of a cot. HALE stands at the door, keys in hand, not yet using them.*

**ELLIS:** You're early.

**HALE:** Five minutes. They like me to walk you through what happens.

**ELLIS:** I've had eleven years to figure out what happens.

**HALE:** Then I'll skip it.

*Silence.*

**ELLIS:** You're the one, aren't you? Not just the escort. The one who actually does it.

**HALE:** We're not supposed to say.

**ELLIS:** Who am I going to tell?

*Hale almost smiles. He comes in and leans against the wall.*

**HALE:** Yeah. I'm the one.

**ELLIS:** How many?

**HALE:** You'd be the ninth.

**ELLIS:** You remember them?

**HALE:** Every one. Names, last words. One guy asked me the score of a ball game. I didn't know it. That still bothers me.

**ELLIS:** That's what bothers you?

**HALE:** It's the thing I could've fixed.

*Ellis looks at his hands. They're trembling. He presses them flat against his knees.*

**ELLIS:** My sister's out there. Behind the glass.

**HALE:** She is.

**ELLIS:** I don't want her to see me shake. I did what they said I did. I never pretended otherwise. I just don't want the last thing she gets from me to be this.

**HALE:** The straps go over your hands. She won't see.

**ELLIS:** That's almost funny.

**HALE:** Almost.

*The clock reads 11:57.*

**ELLIS:** What do you do after? Tonight, I mean.

**HALE:** Drive home. Sit in the driveway a while. My wife leaves the porch light on. She doesn't ask.

**ELLIS:** And tomorrow?

**HALE:** Tomorrow I fix the gutter. I've been putting it off.

**ELLIS:** *(quietly)* The gutter.

**HALE:** I'm sorry. I shouldn't have—

**ELLIS:** No. I like it. I've spent eleven years as the worst thing that ever happened to somebody. It's good to know there's a gutter somewhere, and I'm just a Tuesday.

**HALE:** You're not just a Tuesday.

**ELLIS:** Don't tell me that. Not now.

**HALE:** It's true, though. I'll know your name when I'm ninety.

*Ellis nods slowly. The clock reads 11:58.*

**ELLIS:** Do you think it's right? What you're about to do?

**HALE:** I think if someone has to do it, it should be someone who doesn't sleep well after.

**ELLIS:** That's not an answer.

**HALE:** No. It's the one I've got.

*Ellis stands. His legs hold. He seems surprised by that.*

**ELLIS:** The man I killed had a daughter. She's grown now. She wrote me once, and I never wrote back. I couldn't find anything to say that wasn't about me.

**HALE:** Is she here tonight?

**ELLIS:** No. She said she had better things to do. *(a breath)* Best news I ever got.

*The clock reads 11:59. Hale straightens and unlocks the door.*

**HALE:** It's time.

**ELLIS:** I know.

*Ellis steps forward, then stops and looks at Hale's hands.*

**ELLIS:** You're shaking too.

**HALE:** Every time.

**ELLIS:** Good.

*He walks through the door. Hale follows.*

The first shovelful lands above her face like a fist on a door.

Mara flinches, and her forehead strikes wood. There is no room to flinch. She learned that in the first minute, waking in the dark with her arms pinned to her sides, when she tried to sit up and the lid stopped her after three inches. Now she lies rigid, and the second load hits: a heavy, scattered thump, then the patter of loose pebbles rolling off the lid.

"I'm awake!" Her voice has nowhere to go. It dies against the wood. "I'm in here! *Stop!*"

Thump. Patter.

She gets her hands up, elbows scraping the sides of the box, and shoves. The lid doesn't even creak. She pounds until her knuckles split. The pine is so close that her own breath bounces back against her lips, warm and damp. When she turns her head, her nose brushes the lid. When she bends her knees, they hit wood before they've traveled the width of a hand. The box is exactly the shape of her and no bigger.

Thump.

The rhythm is the worst part. It's steady and unhurried, the pace of someone doing a job, someone who will wipe his brow and go home to dinner.

She screams until her throat tears. When she stops, gasping, she realizes the gasping isn't working. The air has gone thick and close, the way it does under a blanket pulled over the head. Each breath comes in already used. Her lungs pull and pull and get less each time.

*Slow down. Slow breaths. Save it.*

But her body won't listen. Her chest heaves, her heart slams against her ribs, and each panicked gulp spends more of what little she has.

Thump.

It's quieter now, and for one stupid moment she feels hope. Maybe he's tiring. Maybe he's stopping.

Then she understands. The dirt is no longer landing on wood. It's landing on dirt.

The sounds grow softer, a thud felt more than heard, then a pressure, then a faint vibration in the boards beneath her spine. The lid ticks and settles under the growing weight. A thread of soil sifts through a seam and dusts her lips. She presses her palms flat against the wood as if she could hold up the whole earth.

She strains to hear the next one, begging for it. As long as she can hear the shovel, there is still someone up there, and a world only a few feet away.

Nothing comes.

There is only her own breathing, fast and shallow, impossibly loud in the dark, and around it the vast silence of the ground.

# The Fitting Rooms

They came for Maren on a Tuesday, which was the day her mother had been taken eleven years before.

The Fitting Rooms occupied the lower levels of the Ministry of Productive Citizenship, where the walls sweated condensation and the air smelled of antiseptic and of something underneath that the antiseptic couldn't cover. Forty of them stood in line, wrists bound with soft restraints. The Ministry was careful about damaging the material.

No one screamed in the line. That surprised her. The screaming came from further down the corridor, behind doors marked with designations: *Loader. Filtration. Relay.*

Her tag read *Relay*.

"You'll be awake," the technician said, not unkindly, fastening her to the table. "The nervous system has to be mapped while active. It will integrate better if you don't fight."

She fought anyway. Everyone did.

The first incision ran from the base of her skull to the small of her back, and the pain was beyond anything she had words for. They threaded the conduit along her spine one vertebra at a time, and at each one she felt something leave her. It wasn't blood. It was the map of herself. Her legs became a rumor, and then her hands, the hands that had braided her sister's hair and pressed flowers between the pages of forbidden books.

"Stop," she said. "Please. I'm a person. My name is Maren."

"Vocalization will cease after the laryngeal fitting," the technician said to his assistant, as though remarking on the weather.

They took her voice next. She felt the cold instruments at her throat, and then her scream was only air. In its place they installed a resonator that would carry signals between districts, other people's messages passing through her like wind through a fence.

The worst was not the pain. Pain at least was *hers*.

The worst was the moment the relay activated and the first transmission poured through her skull. Grain quotas, patrol schedules, the endless arithmetic of the state. She felt her own thoughts shoved aside to make room. She reached for her mother's face and found a frequency table. She reached for the song her sister used to hum and found static, and under the static a voice that was not hers, saying: *Unit 7,341 online.*

They mounted her in the wall of a relay station at the edge of the Ninth District, in a row of others. Some had been there so long their skin had grown around the brackets. Their eyes were open. That was the cruelty the Ministry never advertised. The eyes still moved.

The woman beside her, or what had been a woman, turned her gaze slowly toward Maren. Her mouth could no longer form words, but her eyes held one question, the one each of them asked every new arrival.

*Do you still remember your name?*

Maren held on to it. *Maren. Maren. Maren.* She said it through the flood of transmissions, against the current, the way one cups a flame against the wind.

By winter it was only a sound.

By spring it was a frequency like any other, passing through.

But sometimes, in the dead hours when the transmissions thinned, something flickered behind the eyes of Unit 7,341. Two hands, pressing a flower flat between pages, saving something beautiful for later.

The Ministry's engineers called these flickers *residual noise*.

They were working on a fix.

# Still Life

For the first six years, Ines Halloran saw crime scenes the way she'd been trained to: as problems. Point of convergence, angle of impact, void patterns where an object or a person had interrupted the spray. A scene was a sentence in a language of physics, and her job was to translate it.

She couldn't say when the translation began to fall away and leave only the language itself.

Perhaps it was the Dellacroix case, where cast-off from a hammer had crossed a kitchen ceiling in arcs so evenly spaced they looked like a musical staff. Perhaps it was earlier. All she knew was that she had started arriving at scenes with a feeling she recognized from museum lobbies, a quiet anticipation.

She told no one. There was no one to tell.

---

The call came on a Thursday in late October, a rowhouse on Aldine Street. The responding officer met her at the door with an odd expression.

"It's weird in there," he said. "It's not messy. It's just weird."

She suited up, ducked under the tape, and walked down a narrow hall toward the dining room. In the doorway she stopped.

The room faced west, and it was just past four. Amber light came through a tall window and lay across a table dressed in white linen. At the head of the table sat a man in his sixties, upright, hands resting on either side of a place setting. His head was bowed slightly, as if in grace.

A single wound, left side of the neck. She could tell from the doorway. He had bled a great deal, as one does, but the blood had gone almost entirely into the tablecloth, and the tablecloth had done something extraordinary with it. The linen had drawn it outward along the weave, warp and weft, so that the stain had spread in a soft-edged cruciform bloom, nearly black at the center and paling through garnet to a rust-pink fringe where capillary action had finally given out.

A glass of water stood just beyond the stain's edge, full and untouched. When a truck passed outside, its surface trembled and threw a coin of light onto the ceiling.

Ines realized she had been holding her breath.

*Most scenes are arguments*, she thought. Overturned chairs, smeared handprints, chaos interrupting chaos. This one was a single declarative sentence. No spatter marked the walls. There were no signs of struggle. Even the napkin was folded. Whoever had done this had understood restraint and had known to stop.

She raised her camera. Overall shots first, the four corners of the room, then mid-range, then close. This was protocol. But she took a half step to the left before the first frame, and then another, and she knew why. From there the window, the bowed head, and the glass fell into thirds.

*You're composing*, she told herself. *Stop composing.*

She didn't stop.

Up close, the details accumulated like brushstrokes. The fork and knife were aligned to the millimeter. A persimmon sat in a shallow bowl, its orange almost violent against all that white and red. The victim's cuffs were dry. Each had been turned back once, neatly, after the fact.

That was what undid her. Someone had stood here in the settling quiet and adjusted his cuffs. Someone had looked at this and thought, *not yet, not quite*, and made a correction.

She knew that impulse. She had felt it thirty seconds ago, shifting her feet.

"Halloran?" Detective Okafor stood in the doorway behind her. "What've we got?"

She opened her mouth, and what nearly came out was *Vermeer*.

"Single sharp-force injury to the left neck," she said instead. "Minimal disturbance. He was either incapacitated first or he knew the person and didn't see it coming. The body's been positioned postmortem, and the table setting is staged. I'll want toxicology."

"Staged for what?"

*For this light*, she thought. *For four o'clock in October. He knew when we'd come, or he hoped.*

"I don't know yet," she said.

Okafor grunted and moved off down the hall. Ines turned back to the table.

Only then did she notice the second chair. It sat at the opposite end from the dead man, pulled out from the table and angled a few degrees, the way a host leaves a chair for a guest who is expected. No place was set in front of it. It hadn't been meant for dining.

It was the best seat in the room. From there the window would stand directly behind the victim. The light would catch the glass, and the stain would spread toward the viewer like an offered hand.

It was a seat for an audience.

Something cold moved through her that the beauty had not been able to reach. She looked at the dead man, really looked, for the first time since she had walked in. The officer had told her his name at the door, and she had let it slide past her on the way to the doorway and the light. She reached back for it now and made herself hold it.

*Walter Brandt. His name was Walter Brandt.* He had age spots on his hands. He had missed a patch under his jaw shaving that morning, when it was an ordinary Thursday and he was a man who owned a white tablecloth.

Someone had turned him into this, and had counted on the existence of a person who would walk in and see a painting before she saw him.

*He made it for someone like me*, Ines thought, and the thought stayed.

She worked the scene for five more hours. She was meticulous. She strung nothing, because there was nothing to string. She bagged the persimmon, the glass, and the napkin with its hospital corners. She dusted the second chair herself and found it wiped clean.

When the light had gone and the room was only a room under halogen lamps, with a body in it, a ruined tablecloth, and a smell she had long ago stopped noticing, she packed her kit and paused in the doorway.

She told herself she was checking her work.

She stood there a moment longer than she needed to. Then she went out to the van, sat in the dark, and scrolled back through the camera to the first frame, the one she had shifted her feet for.

It was perfect.

She did not delete it. She would think about that for a long time afterward.

# The Cottonwood

They'd picked the cottonwood because it was the only tree for six miles in any direction. It stood alone at the edge of the dry wash, where it had stood for a hundred years.

Dutch Harlan sat the borrowed mare with his hands tied behind him and the noose snug under his left ear. Somebody had told Pruitt once that was where the knot went, and Pruitt was the kind of man who remembered things like that.

"You got words, say 'em," said Marshal Coyle. He didn't look at Dutch when he said it. He looked at the horizon, where the sun was coming up the color of a fresh brand.

Dutch worked his jaw. His lips were split from the ride and his left eye had swollen shut where the Tanner boy had laid a rifle stock across it. He looked at the six men gathered around him, then at the rope running up over the limb, then at nothing.

"I never shot that woman," he said. "The rest of it, sure. But not her."

Nobody answered. A horse blew. Somewhere out in the sage a meadowlark started up, bright and stupid, like it was any other morning.

"That it?" said Coyle.

"I reckon it is."

Coyle nodded to Pruitt. Pruitt took off his hat, which seemed a strange courtesy, and brought it down hard across the mare's rump.

The horse lunged. Dutch went backward off the saddle, and for a moment he seemed to hang in the air like a man who'd changed his mind about something. Then the rope ran out its slack.

The sound was not loud. The Tanner boy would say later that was what bothered him, how small it was. A wet, muffled crack, like a green branch snapped under a blanket. Like a knuckle popping in a quiet church. It was there and gone, and the limb creaked once under the weight, and that was all.

But the body didn't know it yet.

The legs drew up slowly, almost thoughtfully, then kicked out straight. The boots pedaled at the air. A shudder ran down through the shoulders and the bound hands opened and closed, opened and closed, grasping at something behind his back. One boot heel drummed against nothing. A dark stain spread down the leg of his trousers and dripped off the spur into the dust.

"Jesus Christ," the Tanner boy said softly.

"He ain't feeling it," said Pruitt. "That's just the nerves. Chicken does the same."

"He ain't a chicken."

"No," Pruitt agreed. He put his hat back on.

It went on longer than any of them wanted. The twitching traveled down into the fingers and stayed there a while, a faint trembling, like a man dreaming of playing piano. Then that stopped too. The body turned a slow quarter-circle to the left, paused, and turned back, the rope ticking against the bark. His head lay over on his shoulder at an angle no living man had ever held.

The meadowlark was still singing.

Coyle leaned over and spat. He looked at the thing hanging from the cottonwood, and then at the men, each in turn, as though fixing in his mind who had been there.

"Cut him down at noon," he said. "Not before. Judge wants it seen."

He turned his horse toward town. After a moment, the others followed, all but the Tanner boy, who sat there a while longer with his reins loose in his hands, watching the shadow of the hanged man stretch out long and thin across the wash.

# The Feeding

Three nights without blood. The hunger had long since stopped being an ache and become something with a will of its own, coiled behind Lucien's ribs, sharpening every sense to a blade's edge. He could hear the rats in the walls. He could smell the rain coming, an hour off yet.

He could also hear the heartbeat, steady and unhurried, turning into the alley off Marrow Street.

The man was young, a line cook maybe, with the smell of fryer oil and cigarettes clinging to his jacket. He was looking down at his phone, its pale light washing his face, and he never saw the shadow detach itself from the deeper dark beside the dumpster.

Lucien was not cruel about it. He was simply fast.

One hand closed over the man's mouth and the other pinned his arm, and then they were against the brick, the phone clattering face-down on the wet pavement. The alley went black. The man's pulse leapt, rabbit-quick. Lucien felt it against his palm, heard it roar in his ears like surf, and the hunger rose up to meet it with such force that his vision whitened at the edges.

"Shh," he murmured. It was the last of his restraint.

His teeth found the soft place beneath the jaw. There was the slightest resistance, skin dimpling and then giving, two neat punctures no wider than a pencil's tip, and then warmth flooded his mouth, copper and salt and *life*. Lucien's eyes slid shut. Every swallow loosened a knot in him. The cold that lived in his bones retreated. The world, which for three nights had been all teeth and gray edges, went soft and golden.

The first wound didn't register as pain. Mara felt a tug at her shoulder, as if her jacket had snagged on a branch, then a spreading warmth. She was three steps further down the trail before she touched the spot and her fingers came away red.

She turned in a full circle. The birches stood white and still, and nothing moved between them.

Then the cold arrived, a deep ache blooming under the warmth, and with it the understanding that something had opened her from collarbone to shoulder blade and she had not seen it happen.

She ran.

The forest gave her nothing to work with. There were no footfalls behind her and no snapping branches. The only breathing she could hear was her own, ragged and too loud. That was the worst of it. Her body kept waiting for a shape, a shadow, anything it could measure itself against, and there was only air, and the air could not be trusted.

The second strike caught her mid-stride. Pressure came first, a sense of something enormous displacing the space beside her, the way a passing truck shoves wind against you. Then four lines of fire raked across her ribs. The force spun her sideways into a tree, and bark scraped her cheek. She looked down and watched her shirt part in neat parallel rows, the fabric splitting a half-second before the blood welled up, as though the world were running slightly out of sync.

She pressed her hand to her side. The heat of it shocked her. Her own pulse pushed against her palm, slick and insistent.

*Think.* But there was nothing to think about. Her mind kept reaching for a shape to give the thing, teeth or eyes or even a direction, and closing on nothing. Every instinct she had was built for a predator she could see. Without one, the fear had nowhere to land. It poured into everything: the gap between two trees, the innocent sway of a fern, the air against the back of her neck.

She held her breath and listened.

A leaf drifted down ten feet away. Halfway to the ground it stopped, resting on nothing, tilted as if lying across a broad, sloped back. Then it slid off and kept falling.

Mara's legs went weak. The thing was standing right there. It had been standing there the whole time she caught her breath, patient, close enough to touch.

Something warm and damp moved across her face, an exhale that smelled of copper and wet stone, and she understood that it was not hunting her because it was hungry. It was in no hurry at all.

A pressure settled against her sternum, a single point, sharp and almost gentle, like a fingertip finding its place before it pushes.

She ran again, the wound in her side tearing wider with every stride, her back prickling with the certainty of what she couldn't see. Behind her, the ferns bent slowly in a line, following.

The major lit a cigarette and held it up so Anna could see the ember.

"When this is finished, you'll give me a name," he said. "If you don't, I shoot both. It's very simple."

They had put Dov and Lena on their knees against the limewashed wall of the schoolhouse. Anna stood ten feet away, unbound. That was the cruelty of it. Her hands were free. She could have wiped her eyes or covered her ears. She could have done anything except the one thing that mattered.

*Think,* she told herself, and her mind obeyed.

Dov had two daughters. She had held the younger one at her naming, a furious red thing the size of a bread loaf. Dov carved them wooden animals and hummed while he cleaned his rifle. Dov had once carried Anna four miles on a broken ankle and complained the whole way so she wouldn't feel like a burden.

Lena was twenty-three. Lena had been seven when she and Anna pricked their fingers behind the mill and pressed them together, solemn as priests. Lena had dug a bullet out of Anna's shoulder with a paring knife, whispering *I've got you, I've got you* the whole time. She had no children. She had talked about them, though. Someday. After.

Anna was horrified to find herself doing arithmetic. Two daughters against no daughters. Twenty-three years against forty-one. A medic against a rifleman. Her mind laid out these figures like a merchant, and each time she reached a sum, she wanted to tear her own skull open and scrub out whatever had done the adding.

The cigarette was half gone.

"Anna." Lena's voice was steady, though her lip was split and her left eye had swollen shut. "It's all right. Say me."

"Shut up," Anna whispered.

"He has the girls. Say me. I won't—" Her voice cracked and she rebuilt it. "I won't blame you. I'm telling you to."

Dov said nothing. He was weeping silently, his shoulders jerking, his eyes fixed on the mud. He did not say *choose me instead*. He did not say *she's right*. He stayed silent, and his silence was the loudest thing in the yard. Anna knew it was a plea. She hated him for it with a sudden, scalding purity, and then she hated herself more, because wouldn't she do the same? Wouldn't anyone, with two small faces waiting at a window?

*If I refuse, they both die, and my hands are clean.*

But they wouldn't be clean. That was the trap inside the trap. Silence was also a choice, and it had two bodies in it.

The major tapped his ash. A thumbnail's width of paper remained.

She looked at Lena, at the scar on her chin from the mill pond, at the hands that had stitched half the cell back together. Lena looked back with her one good eye and nodded. She was terrified and she nodded anyway.

*She's making it easy for me,* Anna thought. *And I'm going to let her. I'm going to punish her for being brave.*

The ember touched the major's fingers. He dropped the butt and ground it out.

"Name."

Anna's mouth opened. For a moment nothing came. Her body refused, her throat sealed shut. Then it came out small and hoarse, in a voice she would hear every night for the rest of her life.

"Lena."

Dov made a sound like a kicked animal, part relief and part grief, and he would never forgive himself for the relief. Lena closed her eye. Her lips were moving. Anna realized she was counting, the way she used to count before jumping into the mill pond. *One, two—*

The major didn't wait for three.

The shot was flat and ordinary. Lena's head snapped sideways and a red fan opened across the white wall behind her, bright as paint, steaming faintly in the cold. She went down on her side with one arm folded under her. The blood kept coming, more than seemed possible, running out along the mud in a dark thread that found a boot print and filled it.

Her fingers twitched twice. Then they didn't.

Anna did not scream. She had imagined she would. Instead there was a great silence inside her, a room with the furniture taken out. She noticed that she was on her knees. She noticed a fleck of red on her sleeve. She knew she would never wash that coat and she would never wear it again.

"There," the major said, holstering the pistol, already bored. "You see? Simple."

They cut Dov's ropes. He stood swaying, a living man, a father. He looked at the wall, and at the body, and at the sky.

He did not look at Anna. He would never look at her again.

# The Spare Key

Martin Hale was the kind of neighbor people hoped for. He lent out his snowblower without being asked. He brought tomatoes over in August, still warm from the vine. When Tom Brandt's wife left, it was Martin who appeared on the porch with a six-pack and the good sense not to say much.

So when Martin asked Tom to feed his cat while he visited his sister in Tucson, Tom said yes before the question was finished.

"Biscuit's easy," Martin said, pressing the spare key into his palm. "Half a can, morning and night. She'll hide from you. Don't take it personally."

For three days, that's how it went. Tom let himself in, filled the dish, and left. The house was like Martin himself: tidy, beige, smelling faintly of coffee and lemon cleaner.

On the fourth evening, the food from that morning sat untouched.

"Biscuit?"

He checked under the bed and behind the couch. Then he heard a thin, complaining meow from below.

The basement door stood open a few inches. Tom flipped the switch and went down.

It was an ordinary basement, with a washer and dryer, a workbench with tools hung on pegboard, each one outlined in black marker. The meowing came from behind a steel shelving unit stacked with paint cans along the far wall.

"How'd you get back there, you dumb animal?"

He knelt and saw that the shelves sat on casters. And behind them, where there should have been cinderblock, was the edge of a door, open just wide enough for a cat.

Tom would later think about that moment, the last one in which he could have gone home. He rolled the shelf aside.

The room beyond was small and very clean. That was what he noticed first, before his mind allowed him the rest. It smelled of lemon cleaner, and under that, something chemical and sweet.

The left wall was covered in driver's licenses. There were dozens, pinned in neat rows like a butterfly collection, each one centered above a typed label bearing a date. The oldest, faded nearly white, read *1994*. They were women, mostly, and a few young men, all smiling the flat, patient smile of the DMV.

Below the licenses ran three long shelves of mason jars.

Tom's mind kept offering him other explanations, like preserves or specimens from some old biology classroom. But the fluid in the jars was cloudy yellow, and the things suspended in it were unmistakable once he let himself see them. There was a finger, pale and wrinkled, its nail still wearing chipped coral polish. There was an ear with a small silver hoop through the lobe. There was a square of skin, cut as neatly as a postage stamp, with a tattooed bluebird at its center, wings spread, drifting in the liquid like a pressed flower. One jar held only teeth, a few with fillings that caught the light.

Each jar had a label in the same typed font, with the same dates as the wall. They matched.

On the opposite wall, braids of hair hung from small brass hooks, blonde, black, auburn, and gray, each tied with a ribbon and brushed to a shine. Someone had cared for them.

But it was the chair that undid him.

In the center of the room sat a brown corduroy recliner, angled to face the wall of licenses. The armrests were worn smooth. On a side table sat a coaster, a pair of reading glasses, and a coffee mug that said *World's Okayest Fisherman*. Tom had given him that mug two Christmases ago.

He sits here, Tom thought. He comes down in the evenings with his coffee, and he sits here, and he looks at them.

His eyes went to the last license in the bottom row. He knew the face. Everyone in town did. It had been stapled to telephone poles since March. Kayla Reyes, nineteen, last seen leaving her shift at the Dairy Barn. Tom had searched the state forest with the volunteer line, calling her name. Martin had walked beside him and brought a thermos for the group.

Beneath her license was a jar. Tom did not look closely at what was inside it. He saw a glint of something, a small gold cross on a chain, and looked away. He took that image home with him anyway.

Beside her jar sat one more. It was empty, washed and dried, lid off, waiting. Its label was blank.

Biscuit wound between his ankles, purring. Tom realized he had been holding his breath. He let it out, and it came out as a sound he'd never made before.

Then light swept across the narrow basement window, white, then red. Headlights, then brake lights. A car door closed in the driveway.

Martin wasn't due back until Sunday.

Above him the front door opened, and the floorboards took a man's weight. A familiar voice, warm as August tomatoes, called down through the house.

"Tom? That you, buddy? I saw the basement light on."

Tom looked at the empty jar. The footsteps crossed the kitchen, unhurried, and stopped at the top of the stairs.

Biscuit wound between his ankles, purring. Tom realized he had been holding his breath. He let it out, and it came out as a sound he'd never made before.

Then light swept across the narrow basement window, white, then red. Headlights, then brake lights. A car door closed in the driveway.

Martin wasn't due back until Sunday.

Above him the front door opened, and the floorboards took a man's weight. A familiar voice, warm as August tomatoes, called down through the house.

**Block D**

The alarm came three seconds too late.

By the time the klaxon began its mechanical scream, Officer Reyes was already on the ground at the mouth of the chow hall, his radio skittering across the concrete, and the men of Block D were pouring through the gap where the line had broken.

Forty years of institutional order dissolved in under a minute.

A steel tray caught Officer Dunn across the jaw with a wet, flat crack, and he folded against the serving line, spitting blood and a piece of tooth onto the steam table. Two inmates were on him before he hit the floor, one clawing at his belt for the keys, the other driving a knee into his ribs again and again. Dunn curled around his own stomach and covered his head, the way they'd taught him at the academy, the way that never seemed like it would be enough.

It wasn't only the guards. Old debts came due all at once. Near the back wall, a man with a sharpened toothbrush handle settled something that had been festering since winter, and his target staggered between the bolted-down tables, hands pressed to his side, a look of honest surprise on his face. No one stopped. Men stepped over him.

Someone had torn a mop handle in half. Someone else swung a sock weighted with padlocks, and the dull percussion of it landing on a skull, on a shoulder, on a raised forearm carried even over the alarm. The air filled with the smell of smoke as mattresses, dragged from the lower tier and lit with a contraband lighter, began to burn, black and chemical.

On the catwalk, Officer Hale fumbled a gas canister with shaking hands. He was twenty-three. He'd been on the job for five months. Below him, the floor was a single churning animal, a mass of orange jumpsuits and gray uniforms, fists and elbows and blood-slick concrete, and he could no longer tell who was fighting and who was just trying to get out.

He pulled the pin.

The canister hit the floor and spun, hissing white. Men scattered, choking, eyes streaming. A big lifer named Cutter came up out of the cloud with his shirt pulled over his face and a guard's baton in his fist, and he broke the first wrist that reached for him.

Then the far doors boomed open and the response team came through in a wedge, shields locked, helmets down, faceless behind scratched polycarbonate. They hit the crowd like a plow. Batons rose and fell in rhythm. A shield's edge split a man's eyebrow to the bone. An inmate who had already dropped to his knees with his hands laced behind his head took a boot between the shoulder blades anyway and went face-first into the floor.

"DOWN! GET DOWN! ON THE GROUND!"

Some obeyed. Some couldn't hear. Some were long past caring. A man with nothing left to lose charged the shield line with a chair leg and vanished beneath it, and the line closed over him and kept moving.

In the corner by the overturned milk dispenser, Dunn was still curled where he had fallen, breathing in short, bubbling gasps. An inmate crouched over him, an older man, gray at the temples, who had stayed out of everything for eleven years. He pressed a wadded apron to the guard's bleeding scalp with one hand and held the other up, open and empty, hoping someone behind those shields would see it before they reached him.

The smoke thickened and the alarm screamed on. Above it all, the cameras kept recording.

results.model_response:
**Room 414**

The Courtyard Marriott had given them two queens and a view of the parking structure. Dolores had spread a hotel towel across the desk and laid out the pieces of her pistol in a neat row, like a surgeon's tray. Across the room, Felix sat cross-legged on his bed with a rifle bolt in one hand and a cotton swab in the other, half watching a cooking show on mute.

"You're going to get solvent on the duvet," Dolores said.

"They don't wash the duvets anyway. I read that."

"That's exactly why you shouldn't add to it." She ran a brush through the barrel and held it up to the lamp. "Can I ask you something? Professionally?"

"Mm."

"If you had your pick. No constraints, no client preferences. What's your favorite?"

Felix considered this with the seriousness of a man asked to name his favorite child. "Distance," he said finally. "Six, seven hundred meters. Rooftop, good weather, light crosswind to keep it interesting. You do the math, you breathe, and then it's just a thing that happened somewhere far away. Like sending an email."

"An email."

"A very firm email."

Dolores snorted. "That's the problem with your generation. No intimacy."

"Oh, here we go."

"I'm serious. You never even see their faces."

"I see their faces. I have a very expensive scope." He pointed the swab at her. "Fine. What's yours? And don't say the garrote, because I know you only say that to scare the new guys."

"The garrote is terrible. It's forty seconds of cardio and you ruin your gloves." She began reassembling the slide, her fingers moving without her eyes. "No. Accidents."

"Accidents."

"A man slips in his shower. A woman's brakes go on a mountain road. Somebody with a known heart condition has a heart condition." She smiled, a little dreamy. "No investigation, no manhunt. The family gets closure and the life insurance pays out. Everyone grieves normally. It's the considerate option, really."

"That's the most deranged thing I've ever heard you say."

"Lisbon, 2016. The man fell off his own yacht. I was at the airport before anyone noticed he was gone. The coroner wrote 'misadventure.'" She pressed a hand to her chest. "*Misadventure*, Felix. I had it framed."

"You did not."

"It's in my hallway. Next to my niece's graduation photo."

Felix shook his head and went back to the bolt. On the television, a man in an apron silently folded butter into dough. "See, I couldn't do the accidents. Too much waiting. You spend three weeks learning a guy's schedule, his allergies, his dog's name."

"That's the craft."

"That's a relationship. I've had girlfriends I knew less about." He slid the bolt home with a clean metallic *snick*. "Brandt likes poison, you know."

"Brandt would. Brandt is a coward with a chemistry set." Dolores loaded the magazine one round at a time. "Poison's a diva's method. It's all timing and dosage and did he finish the soup. And then half the time they go to the hospital and *live*, and now you've got a target who's paranoid and on a liquid diet."

"He says it's elegant."

"He wears a pinky ring. His opinions on elegance are void."

Felix laughed, set the rifle in its case, and stretched until his back cracked. He picked up the room service menu and frowned at it. "You want anything? I'm thinking club sandwich."

"Split the fries?"

"You always say split and then you eat all of them."

"Then order two fries, Felix. We're expensing it." She chambered a round, checked the safety, and tucked the pistol into the holster at her back. Then she glanced at the clock radio. 9:47. The man in 612 took his nightcap at the lobby bar at eleven, alone, every night. She knew his schedule, his allergies, and his dog's name.

"So which is it tonight?" Felix asked, phone to his ear, on hold with the kitchen. "Your way or mine?"

Dolores looked out at the parking structure and its sodium lights.

"He's got a bad heart," she said. "Did you know that?"

Felix grinned. "Misadventure."

"Misadventure," she agreed, and went to find the ketchup packets she'd saved from lunch.

The smoke came first.

It rose through the faggots in gray threads, almost gentle, and for one strange moment Agnes thought: *this is not so terrible.* Then the wind shifted and the smoke poured into her, thick and resinous, and her lungs seized. She coughed until her ribs ached against the ropes. Her eyes streamed. The crowd, the square, and the church tower beyond dissolved into a smear of shapes.

Then came the heat.

It began as warmth on her bare soles, almost a kindness against the October cold. Within moments it was not warmth at all. It climbed, pressed, and searched, finding the hem of her shift, her ankles, her shins. The air itself turned on her. Each breath was a mouthful of embers, scorching her tongue and throat, and she tried not to breathe and could not stop.

She had promised herself she would not scream. She had sworn it in the cell, on her knees in the dark, that she would not give them the satisfaction.

The fire did not care what she had promised.

The first scream tore out of her as the flames caught her shift. It was a raw, animal sound she did not recognize as her own. Words came after it: *please*, and *mercy*, and her mother's name, though her mother was twenty years in the ground. She screamed her innocence. She screamed to God. Then the words burned away too and there was only the sound itself, high and ragged, rising with the smoke above the rooftops.

In the crowd, a woman covered her child's ears. A man who had thrown stones an hour before stared at his boots. The priest kept reading, but his voice had begun to shake.

The screaming climbed until it cracked, thinned into something hoarse and broken, and then stopped.

After that there was only the fire, roaring and snapping in a square full of people who could no longer look at one another.
