results.model_response:
The battle of Harrow Ford was three weeks over, and the dead had gone soft.

Tam held the lantern as he'd been told, high and steady, though his arm shook. The field stretched out below the ridge, a thousand shapes slumped in the mud. The crows had long since taken the eyes. The bellies had swollen and burst and sunk. The smell was sweet and thick, like a butcher's midden in August, and it had weight. It coated his tongue.

Mother Ilsabet stood at the edge of the slope with her sleeves rolled to the elbow, like a midwife.

"Don't run," she said. "Whatever happens, the light stays still."

Then she began to speak.

Tam had expected chanting. This was quieter and much worse, a low, patient muttering, like someone reciting a debt. The words did not echo off the ridge. They sank into the ground like water into sand, and where they sank, the grass went gray.

The lantern flame bent toward her, against the wind.

Tam's teeth began to ache, down to the roots. He tasted old coins. His shadow slid slowly around his feet until it pointed at the light instead of away from it, and some animal part of him, older than thought, began to scream that he should not be here, that nothing should be here.

The flies left first. They rose from the field in a single black sheet and fled. Then the maggots came, pouring out of the bodies in pale streams, writhing away through the mud. Even the worms would not stay for this.

The first corpse moved.

It did not wake. Tam would have nightmares about that for the rest of his life. A sleeper wakes all at once, with breath and a flutter of the eyes. This thing was pulled. Its chest jerked upward as if hooked through the breastbone, and the limbs followed in the wrong order, elbow before shoulder, knee before hip, the head lolling on a neck gone the color of a bruised plum. When it stood, part of it did not. The skin of its back stayed in the mud where it had lain, and what was left of its belly slid out through the split in its mail and landed wetly at its feet.

It did not notice. It stood there, leaking.

Then another rose, then a dozen. Soon the whole field was heaving, a thousand ruined men dragged upright by nothing. Flesh hung from their forearms like wet sleeves. Jaws dangled from single hinges. One had been lying facedown in the ford, and its face was white and bloated, the features run together like wax. The rot was not mending. It had only stopped, held in place like a breath.

There was no groaning. The only sounds were the creak of gristle and the muttering, which continued a full three seconds after Mother Ilsabet closed her mouth.

A thousand eyeless faces turned toward her.

"There," she said, wiping her hands on her apron. She looked older. The gray in the grass had spread to the ridge, and Tam realized he could no longer remember the sound of his own mother's voice. It was simply gone, taken as payment. "Empty as jugs, every one. Nothing left inside to trouble them."

Tam nodded. He did not trust himself to speak.

Near the front of the ranks, one of the dead men had lifted its hand. Slowly, clumsily, with fingers worn down to bone and tatters, it was patting the breast of its rotted tabard, over and over. It was searching for something it had once kept there, a letter perhaps, or a lock of hair.

Mother Ilsabet had already turned away, and Tam did not tell her.

**Blood In**

The Buick idled at the curb with its headlights off. Marcus sat in the back seat, wedged between two bodies that smelled of weed and sweat. No one had spoken in ten minutes.

Dre finally turned around in the passenger seat. He was twenty-six, ancient by the standards of the set, with a scar that pulled his left eyelid slightly down. He held out an aluminum bat, grip first.

"That's him." He nodded at the bus stop across the street, where a kid in a red hoodie stood looking at his phone. "Hangs with them Eastside boys. Been walking through our blocks like he owns the sidewalk."

Marcus looked. The kid couldn't have been older than sixteen. His own age.

"He's just standing there," Marcus said.

The car went quiet, and he knew at once it had been the wrong thing to say.

"Just standing there." Dre repeated it slowly. "You hear this? Lil' homie wants to file a report." Nobody laughed. Dre leaned closer and his voice dropped, almost gentle. "Listen to me. Everybody in this car did what you're about to do. Everybody. Tiny did his at fourteen. You think you're better than Tiny?"

"No."

"You been eating with us four months. Wearing the colors. Telling people you're with us." Dre pressed the bat against Marcus's chest until he took it. "That was credit. Tonight you pay it back. You get out and handle that, or you get out and keep walking. But understand what walking means. You know our names. You know our faces. You know where we keep things." He let that sit. "We can't have somebody like that out there who isn't one of us. You feel me?"

Marcus felt him. It was the same threat he'd watched them carry out on a boy named Chris, who now ate through a straw.

Tiny reached across and opened the door. The dome light had been disabled. They had done this before.

"Clock's running, young blood."

The bat was lighter than he expected. He crossed the street on legs that seemed to belong to someone else. The kid looked up when Marcus was ten feet away, and for half a second they just saw each other. The kid's face moved through confusion, then recognition of the colors, then a fear so naked it looked like childhood.

"Yo, hold on, I don't even—"

The first swing caught him across the forearm he'd thrown up, and Marcus felt the crack travel up the bat into his own hands. The kid screamed and went down on one knee. Behind him, from the car, someone was whooping. Someone was filming.

*Stop*, said something inside him. But the car was back there, and Dre was back there, and stopping now meant he'd have done this for nothing, so he swung again. The ribs. The shoulder. The kid curled on the pavement trying to make himself small, saying *please* over and over, then just sounds. The bat came down across his back, his hip, the hand shielding his head. There was a noise like a branch breaking in wet weather.

Then arms were around Marcus, pulling him back, and he realized he was still swinging at the air.

"That's enough, that's enough. Look at this fool, he's a *animal*!" Dre was laughing, dragging him to the car, and the others were slapping his back, his neck, his head. The Buick pulled away, and through the rear window Marcus watched the red hoodie on the sidewalk get smaller, not moving, one sneaker lying a few feet from the rest of him.

"You're family now," Dre said, clamping a hand on the back of his neck. "Blood in. Can't nobody take that from you."

Marcus nodded. His hands wouldn't stop shaking, and he sat on them so no one would see. There was a spot of something on his wrist, and he rubbed it against his jeans until the skin burned.

Everyone was laughing. He made his face laugh too.

Later he would understand that this was the real initiation. It wasn't the bat. It was the laughing afterward, and the car pulling away, and the door inside him that he had to close and hold shut for the rest of his life.

# The Last Course

Thirty-one years of marriage, and Desmond has never once complimented my cooking without attaching a correction. Tonight is no different.

"The stew is good," he says, tearing his bread. "Bit heavy-handed with the pepper."

"Is it?" I lift my wine glass. "I'll remember that for next time."

There's no pepper in it at all. That tingle on his tongue is something else entirely, something from the blue flowers along the garden wall, the ones he told me to rip out last spring because they made the yard look untidy. I've always been a patient gardener.

He eats the way he does everything: efficiently, without pleasure, as though the meal were a task to be completed. I watch the spoon travel from bowl to mouth and I count. Four. Five. Six.

"I spoke to the realtor again," he says. "She thinks we can list by March."

"The lake house."

"We've been over this, Margaret." He doesn't look up. "It's a building. Your father's been dead twenty years. Sentiment doesn't pay the taxes."

"No," I agree. "I suppose it doesn't."

He works his lips together, a small, unconscious smacking, then drags the napkin across his mouth. A moment later he does it again. I know from my reading that the tingling comes first, a fizzing in the lips and tongue like sparkling wine gone wrong. Then the numbness spreads behind it like frost across a window.

"Did you change the recipe?" He runs his tongue over his teeth.

"Just a little something from the garden."

He grunts and keeps eating. Of course he does. In thirty-one years Desmond has never left a plate unfinished or a thought of mine unexamined for flaws. He drains his water glass, and I rise to refill it like the good wife I have always been.

"Claire called today," I say, sitting back down.

That's a lie. Claire hasn't called in six years, not since the Christmas he told her what he thought of her choices, her husband, her life. But I want to say her name in this room while he can still hear it.

"Did she." He flexes his right hand, opening and closing the fingers, frowning at them as if they belonged to someone else. "What did she want? Money?"

"She wanted to know how I was."

His spoon clatters against the rim of the bowl. He stares at it, picks it up, and I watch his fingers fumble at the handle like a man wearing thick gloves. A fine sheen has risen along his hairline, and his face has gone the color of candle wax.

"It's freezing in here," he mutters. "Did you touch the thermostat?"

"No, dear."

"Well, something's—" He stops and swallows hard, his throat working. He presses his palm flat against his breastbone, and for the first time I see something flicker behind his eyes. It isn't fear yet. Desmond has never believed anything could happen to him that he didn't authorize. It's only confusion, the look of a man whose own body has begun speaking a language he doesn't know.

I know what he's feeling. His heart, so steady and joyless all these years, has begun to stumble, a beat dropped, then three in a rush, like someone falling down stairs.

"Margaret." My name comes out thick and slurred at the edges. His tongue is a stranger in his mouth now. "I don't feel right."

"You've been working too hard." I fold my napkin beside my plate. My own bowl is still full. He never noticed I wasn't eating, but then he never noticed much about me at all. "You should rest."

He tries to push back from the table, but his arms have lost their argument with gravity. The chair scrapes an inch and stops. His breathing has turned shallow and quick, and sweat drips from his chin onto the tablecloth my mother embroidered, the one he always called fussy.

"Call..." His lips can barely shape the word. "Call someone."

"I will," I promise, and I mean it. I'll call in a while, when it's finished. I'll weep on the phone. I've had decades of practice at producing the emotion required of me.

His eyes find mine across the table, wide now, and finally seeing. I watch him understand, about the stew and the garden, and perhaps about the lake house, and Claire, and every swallowed word of thirty-one years.

I take a sip of wine and hold his gaze.

"You were right about the pepper, though," I tell him gently. "I do have a heavy hand."

The candles burn lower. Outside, the blue flowers nod against the garden wall. I sit with my husband through the last course, the way a good wife should.

results.model_response:
# The Plank

The sun hung low and red over the Caribbean, laying a road of fire across the water. Captain Isolde Vane stood at the rail of the *Widow's Mercy* with her hands clasped behind her back, watching the fins.

There were four of them now. There had been two an hour ago, when the cook first began ladling slaughterhouse slops over the side.

"Bring him up."

They dragged Tobias Crewe from the hold with his wrists bound in tarred rope. Three days ago he had been quartermaster, a man who laughed loudly and was owed money by half the crew. Three days ago he had stood outside the captain's cabin with a pistol and eleven men at his back. Nine of those men were dead. Two had turned on him before the powder smoke cleared, and they stood among the crew now, studying their boots.

"Isolde," Crewe said. His voice cracked on her name. "Captain. Six years I've sailed with you."

"Six years," she agreed. "And on the first night of the seventh, you came to cut my throat."

The plank was already laid, a length of rough pine lashed to the gunwale and jutting eight feet over the swells. Crewe saw it, and something went out of his legs. The men holding him had to haul him upright.

"Shoot me," he whispered. "God's sake, hang me. Not this. *Not this.*"

Vane said nothing. She nodded to the bosun, who prodded Crewe forward with the point of a cutlass.

He climbed onto the plank the way a man climbs a gallows, because the steel behind him was certain and the death ahead of him was, for a few more seconds, only a possibility. The wood flexed under his weight. He could hear his own breath, quick and shallow, and the creak of the rigging, and beneath it all the soft slap of water against the hull.

He made the mistake of looking down.

The sea was clear enough to see them whole, long gray shapes sliding through the green, unhurried, patient as creditors. One rolled as it passed beneath him, and he saw the pale belly, the black coin of an eye that held nothing at all.

His bladder let go. Nobody laughed.

"Please." He turned his head, and tears cut clean tracks through the grime on his face. "I'll go ashore. Maroon me. I'll never—"

"Every man here is watching, Tobias," Vane said, almost gently. "That's the point of you now. It's the only use you have left."

The bosun stamped on the plank.

Crewe fell with a scream that the water cut short. For a moment there was only a ring of white foam, and the crew leaned over the rail despite themselves. Then he surfaced, gasping, kicking, his bound hands clawing uselessly at the hull's slick planking.

The fins turned as one.

The first shark struck him low and took him under mid-scream. He came up again, impossibly, his mouth a wide black hole, and the water around him was no longer green. The second hit from the side with a force that lifted him half out of the sea, shaking him the way a dog shakes a rat. Something tore. The scream became a wet, choking sound, and then stopped.

After that there was only the water, boiling red and white, with tails thrashing and gray backs rolling over one another in the froth. A scrap of blue cloth floated up and spun there a moment before a blunt snout took that too.

It lasted less than a minute. The stain spread, thinned, and began to drift astern.

The crew stood silent. One of the younger hands was sick over the side.

Captain Vane turned from the rail and let her gaze travel slowly across every face on deck, lingering longest on the two men who had changed sides.

"Pull in the plank," she said. "And set a course for Tortuga."

# What the Water Keeps

For the first three days after he drowned Elias in the quarry lake, Tom Calder felt nothing at all, and he took that as proof he would get away with it.

On the fourth night, he woke to the sound of dripping.

He checked every tap in the house. All of them were dry. But the sound followed him from room to room, slow and patient, and when he returned to bed he found footprints on the hallway boards. They were bare and wet, and they led to the side of his mattress, where they stopped. Nothing led away.

He told himself he'd tracked the water in himself. He told himself many things that week.

By the second week, the water in his glass tasted of silt. He poured it out and watched something thin and green slide down the drain. He stopped drinking from the tap. Then he stopped drinking much at all, and his lips cracked, and still he woke each morning with his pillow soaked through and the smell of lake-bottom in his hair.

That was when he began seeing Elias.

At first it was never directly. He saw a shape in the window glass, standing just behind his own reflection, and a pale smear at the end of the corridor that was gone when he turned. Once, shaving, he looked up and the face in the mirror was not his. It was swollen and gray, the eyes clouded like milk-glass, the mouth hanging open and full of black water that spilled and spilled and never emptied.

He broke the mirror with his fist. He picked the glass from his knuckles and saw the face again in every shard.

What he could not stop remembering, the thing that played behind his eyes whenever he closed them, was not the struggle. It was that there had barely been one. Elias had thrashed for a moment, and then his hand had come up through the water and found Tom's wrist. He had not clawed at it. He had patted it, twice, gently, the way you calm a frightened animal. Then the hand had gone slack.

"Why did you do that?" Tom screamed at the empty kitchen in the third week. He had not slept in four days. He had nailed blankets over the windows and turned every picture to the wall. "Why didn't you fight me? Why didn't you *fight*?"

**Three a.m.**

The rain had quit trying to wash this town clean. Smart rain.

She was lying where the alley ran out of excuses, wedged between a dumpster and a wall that had been sweating the same brown water since Truman. Somebody had taken their time with her. Somebody had opened her up the way the city opens up a street: carelessly, the job left half-done, with no intention of ever putting things back the way they were.

I lit a cigarette I didn't want. It beat breathing the air straight.

The blood had gone the color of old brick. It had found the cracks in the pavement and followed them, the way everything in this town follows the cracks eventually. Money. Rain. People. By morning it'd be down in the storm drains with everything else this city swallows and never digests.

The flies had already found her. They're the only ones in this town who show up on time.

Her face was the worst part, because he'd left it alone. Twenty-five, maybe. Pretty, the way a condemned building is pretty when the light catches its last unbroken window. Her nails were torn down to the quick. She'd fought. Good for her. It hadn't mattered, but good for her.

I've seen what this city does to people. It usually doesn't work this fast. It's a slow rot, damp in the walls, rust blooming under fresh paint. It takes a little each day and sends you home with what's left, and you call that a living. Whoever did this just got impatient. He finished in one night what the city would've needed thirty years to do.

Somewhere above me, a window lit up, then went dark again. Somebody had looked. Somebody had decided not to see. That's the real mold in this place. Not the kind that grows in the tenements, but the kind that grows behind the eyes.

Twenty-two years I've been doing this. People ask if you get used to it. You don't. You just spoil slower than the rest, like meat in a cold room.

I flicked the cigarette into a puddle and listened to it die.

Then I crouched down next to her and went to work.

results.model_response:
**Hour Eleven**

The clock on Mara's wrist read 11:38 when her legs stopped listening to her.

She had made it through the drowned streets of the cannery district, past the rusted hulls where the first two runners had gone down before noon. She had heard their horns, the long, low note the drones played when a tag went dark. She had not stopped. Every hour on the clock was a year of water credits for Deshi. Eleven years. He'd be nineteen by the time they ran out. Nineteen was old enough.

*Twelve,* she told herself. *Give him twelve.*

The wire took her at the ankle.

She hit the concrete hard, palms first, and the taste of copper filled her mouth. Above her, the camera drones tightened their orbit, their lenses glittering like the eyes of patient birds. Somewhere, in the towers across the bay, ten million people leaned toward their screens.

She tried to crawl. The wire held.

Footsteps came, unhurried. Two sets. The tracker came first, a lean woman in gray who never looked at Mara's face, only checked the snare and nodded once. Then the hunter.

He was older than she'd expected. Soft around the jaw, his jacket crisp, sponsor patches stitched down one sleeve. He was breathing hard behind his filter mask, and she realized with distant amazement that he was *tired*. That he considered this exertion.

"Eleven hours, forty-one minutes," he said, reading her wrist. His voice was pleasant. It was the voice of a man complimenting a meal. "That's the best run this season. You should be proud."

Mara spat blood onto his boot.

He looked down at it, then laughed. He wasn't cruel about it, and that was the worst part. He laughed the way you'd laugh at a dog that snapped at you through a fence.

"Spirit," he said to the tracker. "They told me the Sector Nines had spirit."

He knelt. From his belt he drew the claiming knife, a ceremonial thing with a bone handle and a gold-chased blade that had never cut anything but straps. He took her wrist almost gently and slid the blade under the band of her clock. The numbers froze as the strap parted.

11:41.

He held it up to the drones, and the drones dipped in salute, and the horn began to sound across the district. From the towers, faint as surf, she could hear the cheering.

"My name is Mara Okonkwo-Reyes," she said.

The hunter paused. For the first time, something uncomfortable crossed his face.

"They don't broadcast audio at this stage," he said. "No one can hear you."

"You can."

He stood. He tucked her clock into his breast pocket, where it would ride home with him to a glass case, a little brass plate, a story for dinner guests. The tracker handed him the rifle, and he checked it with the careful, practiced motions of someone who had paid for lessons.

"Eleven years of credits," he said, as if it were a kindness. "Your family will be very comfortable."

Mara rolled onto her back. Past the drones, past the smog, there was one pale star, or maybe a satellite. She decided it was a star.

*Nineteen,* she thought. *He'll be nineteen.*

"Mara Okonkwo-Reyes," she said again, and kept saying it. She said it over the horn, over the cheering, over the soft click of the safety, so that whatever else he took home, he would have to take that too.

results.model_response:
**The Spade**

The raid came at a quarter past three, in the dead hour when even the rats went quiet.

Private Alfred Marsh was scraping mud from the firing step when the first grenade went off down the traverse. The blast punched the air from the trench. Then came shouting in two languages, the flat crack of a revolver, and a scream that went on too long.

His rifle was leaning against the parados six feet away. It might as well have been in Sheffield.

The German came around the corner of the traverse fast and low, a shape against the flare-light, and Alfred had only what was in his hands. The entrenching tool. He'd sharpened its edge himself, the way the old hands had shown him. *The bayonet sticks in the ribs, lad. The spade doesn't stick.* He had nodded along as if it were advice about planting potatoes.

The German had a club studded with nails. He swung it and Alfred lurched back, felt it pass his face, and his boots slid in the muck. They crashed together against the trench wall, too close to swing, grappling like drunks. Alfred could smell him: sweat, wet wool, and tobacco, a sweeter tobacco than theirs. The man was grunting something through his teeth, the same word over and over. It might have been a curse. It might have been a prayer.

The German's foot slipped on the duckboard. It was nothing, half a second of lost balance, but it opened a space between them, and Alfred's arms filled that space without consulting him.

The spade caught the man where the neck meets the shoulder.

The sound was the worst of it. Alfred had split kindling all his life, and it was not like that. It was wetter and more intimate, and he felt it travel up the handle into his wrists. The German dropped to his knees. His club fell. He put one hand up, not to fight but the way a man does when he wants a moment to think, and looked at Alfred with an expression of profound surprise.

Alfred hit him again, and again. Something had taken hold of his arms, something old that lived beneath his name and his mother's hymns and everything he'd believed about himself. The man was down in the mud and Alfred was still swinging, sobbing with each blow, because the man was still making a sound, a low bubbling wheeze, and it had to stop. It was the only thing in the world that mattered. It had to stop.

Then it stopped.

The raid was over in four minutes. Someone told him that later. Flares hissed overhead. Down the line, Sergeant Coyle was calling the roll in a steady voice, as though counting sheep.

Alfred stood over the thing he had made.

The helmet had come off. The man had fair hair, thinning at the crown, and that was what undid him. Not the wound, which his eyes refused to settle on, but the thinning hair. This man had stood before a mirror and worried about going bald. He had a wife, perhaps, who teased him for it. He was thirty-five or forty, old enough to be someone's father, and there was a button missing from his tunic, sewn over with thread that didn't quite match.

Alfred's hands would not open. He looked down at them, white-knuckled around the handle, and told them to let go, and they would not. He was shaking so hard his teeth clicked, and a high thin noise was coming from somewhere. It took him a moment to understand it was coming from him.

"Marsh." Coyle was beside him. The sergeant glanced down, and his face did nothing at all. "You hurt?"

Alfred tried to say no. What came out instead was his breakfast, yesterday's bully beef, splashing down the trench wall. Coyle waited, a hand on his back, patient as a man holding a gate.

"First one's the worst," Coyle said. Then, quieter: "That's a lie. But say it to yourself anyway."

They pried his fingers off the handle one at a time.

Afterward he sat on the firing step with a mug of rum-laced tea he could not hold steady. Two stretcher-bearers took the German away, a blanket over the ruin. One limp hand trailed out from under it, and on the hand was a ring.

The spade lay where it had fallen. At some point, someone cleaned it and propped it beside his kit, because a tool was a tool and there was a sap to be dug tomorrow.

Alfred looked at his hands. They looked the same. That seemed to him the most terrible thing, that they were the hands that had buttered bread and held Mary Ellison's waist at the Whitsun dance and turned the pages of his father's Bible. He kept waiting to feel like a murderer, or a soldier, or anything with a name. He felt only the vibration in his wrists, as if the handle were still there. He would feel it, on and off, for the next fifty years.

At dawn the birds began singing over no man's land, as they always did, and he hated them for it.

## The World

In the Commonwealth of Harrow, there is only one crime. The Parity Statutes, passed during the famine years, abolished the old distinctions between murder and arson, between trespass and theft. Every offense is a theft from the common order, the reasoning goes, and a thief who takes a little differs from a thief who takes a lot only in ambition. So there is one crime and one penalty.

The executions are called Reckonings. They are held on the sixth day of each week in every district square, and attendance is compulsory. Ration cards are stamped at booths that open only when the Reckoning concludes. No stamp, no bread.

The square had filled by noon, as it always did. People stood where they always stood, the tannery families near the fountain, the mill workers along the east wall, having learned over the years where the sightlines were worst.

A man sold roasted chestnuts from a cart by the clock tower. He did good business. People liked to have something to do with their hands.

The boy they brought out was sixteen, though he looked younger in the gray smock. A murmur passed through the crowd. It was not protest, since Harrow had forgotten how to make that sound, but a kind of flinch given voice. Someone's grandmother said, "Oh, he's small," and her daughter gripped her arm until she was quiet.

The Magistrate read the charge. *One loaf, wheaten, taken from the premises of Aldous Brandt, baker, on the ninth day of the month.* Brandt stood in the witnesses' row at the front, as the law required. He was a big man, and he had made himself as small as he could, his eyes fixed on his own shoes. He had not reported the theft. A neighbor had. Everyone knew this, and everyone also knew that the neighbor's ration had been doubled for the month, and no one stood near her now. She stood in a little clearing of her own making, chin raised, daring anyone to look at her. No one did.

"The Commonwealth is a single body," the Magistrate said. "What is taken from one is taken from all."

"So is it reckoned," the crowd answered.

Nearly two thousand people said it together, and that was the trick of it. In so large a sound, no one could tell who spoke and who only moved their lips. A dyer's wife near the fountain had not made a sound at a Reckoning in four years. Her husband knew. He said the words loudly enough for both of them.

A father lifted his young daughter onto his shoulders, not so she could see, but because the wardens watched for children hidden in coats. He had told her it was a kind of play. She was nearly old enough to stop believing him, and he felt her go still as the boy climbed the steps.

Tobin Hale did not make a speech. They never did; it wasn't permitted. But he looked out at the crowd, searching it, and the crowd did what it had trained itself to do. It looked at the clock tower, the chestnut cart, the back of the next person's head. Two thousand people in a square, and the boy could not find a single pair of eyes.

Except one. Near the mill wall, an old man had taken off his cap. It was a small, obsolete gesture from a time when deaths were mourned. A warden marked it. The old man's neighbors edged away from him by inches, the way water withdraws from a stone.

Then came the sound of the trap. Everyone in Harrow knew that sound the way they knew the mill whistle. The crowd made its own sound in answer, a single breath pulled through two thousand throats and held.

On her father's shoulders, the little girl said, clearly, in the silence, "But when does he get up?"

No one answered her. Her father lifted her down and pressed her face into his coat.

Then the bell rang, the stamping booths opened their shutters, and the crowd exhaled and turned. This was the part that visitors from other districts never forgot. No one cheered or wept. Everyone shuffled to form lines, cards held ready. The crowd was most alive in the first minute after, in the relief of having something to queue for. Neighbors murmured about the weather. The chestnut seller sold out.

Brandt the baker stood where he was until a warden moved him along.

By evening the square was empty. The old man who had removed his cap did not return to his rooms that night, and his neighbors did not ask after him.

But in the morning, when the sweepers came, they found something at the foot of the scaffold, set there in the dark by a hand no one had seen: a loaf of bread, whole and untouched. In a hungry city, no one had dared to take it.

**THE THRESHOLD**

*A monologue. FATHER ELIAS stands before his congregation in a lamplit barn. He speaks softly. He has never needed to shout.*

---

Sit. Sit, my children. Let me look at you.

*(He takes his time. He smiles.)*

Eleven years. Some of you have been with me eleven years. Miriam, you came to us with nothing but a suitcase and a bruise you wouldn't explain. Do you remember what I told you that night? I said, *you are home now.* And was I lying?

Was I ever lying?

They called you broken out there. Your families. Your doctors. Your bosses. They looked at the most luminous souls I have ever known and saw problems to be managed. I am the only one who saw you. Remember that tonight. Whatever else you feel tonight, remember who saw you.

*(He moves among them, touching a shoulder, a cheek.)*

I know some of you are afraid. Thomas, I can see it, and it's all right. Fear is just the body talking. The body is a loyal animal, and it does not want to be left behind. But we have never been bodies, have we? Haven't I taught you that? Haven't we spent every morning for eleven years learning to hear the signal beneath the noise?

The signal has never been louder than it is tonight.

*(His voice drops.)*

You've seen the cars at the end of the road. You know what's coming. They will come through that gate with their papers and their cameras, and they will scatter us. They will put you back in those gray rooms and gray lives and call it rescue. They will take the children and teach them to forget. They will tell you that everything we've built here was a sickness.

The window is closing. I did not choose the hour. I would have given you a hundred more summers here if it were mine to give. But the door is open *now*, and it will not stay open, and I will not, I *cannot*, walk through it and leave even one of you behind.

*(A pause. Something harder enters his voice.)*

Now. Someone in this room is thinking: *what if he's wrong?*

I know, because doubt is the world's last hook in you. So ask yourself where that voice comes from. Is it the part of you that woke up here, or the part that was dying out there? Every one of you has trusted me with everything. Your savings. Your names. Your children. And have I not carried it? Have I not carried *all* of it?

I'm asking you to trust me one more time. One last time. And then never again, because where we're going, there will be no need for trust. Only knowing.

*(He softens again and opens his arms.)*

We will go together. That's the gift. No one in the history of this sad world gets to go *together*, and we do. Hand in hand, the way we've done everything.

They'll say terrible things about us tomorrow. Let them. They've never understood a single thing we've done.

*(He looks toward the door, where the faint sound of engines can be heard. He turns back and smiles.)*

Come, my children. Come close.

It's time to go home.

---

He conflates love with debt ("remember who saw you"), manufactures urgency, recasts doubt as contamination, and frames outside help as persecution. Real coercive leaders like Jim Jones used the same techniques. I can adjust the tone, setting, or theology, or make his manipulation more or less visible, depending on the piece.*

The smell reached Nora before she'd even gotten the key out of the lock. In the hallway it was only a suggestion, something sweetish and wrong, like garbage left out in August. When the door swung open, it became a wall.

She actually stepped back. The smell was thick enough to feel like a physical thing, warm and wet, pressing into her nose and mouth. It was sweet, which was the worst part, a syrupy rot layered over something sulfurous and fecal, like spoiled meat and sewage with a cloying edge of cheap perfume. She pulled her collar over her face and it made no difference. She could taste it, coating her tongue and the back of her throat.

"Mr. Halvorsen?"

The apartment was stifling, the radiator ticking. Flies crawled along the inside of the windows in sluggish dozens. More of them drifted in lazy circles near the bathroom door, which stood open a few inches.

She pushed it with two fingers.

Her mind refused the shape in the tub at first. It registered as a pile of dark, wet laundry. Then the details assembled themselves against her will.

He had swollen to nearly twice his size, his abdomen drum-tight, his limbs filling the tub like something inflated. The skin had gone a mottled green-black, and across his shoulders and chest the veins stood out in dark, branching lines, like marble or rivers on a map. His face was no longer a face she knew. The features were bloated smooth, the lips ballooned and parted around a protruding tongue, the eyelids bulging. Dark fluid had run from his nose and mouth and dried in streaks down his chin.

The water he lay in had turned the color of strong tea, with a greasy film on its surface. Where his arm rested against the porcelain, the skin had slipped loose in a translucent sheet, like a wet glove half pulled off. Pale things moved at his hairline and in the corners of his eyes.

Her stomach clenched and her mouth flooded with saliva. She made it to the hallway before she vomited, one hand braced against the wall. Even then, with her eyes streaming, the smell was in her hair, in her clothes, and in every breath she dragged in. Some animal part of her understood that she would be smelling it for days, and remembering it for the rest of her life.

---

Dale Pruitt was halfway through a microwave dinner when the garage door rattled up on its own.

He knew before he turned around. Three weeks late, eleven hundred short. He'd been doing the math in his sleep.

"Marco." He set the fork down like it might go off. "I was gonna call you."

"Sure you were." Marco stepped in out of the rain, shaking water from his jacket. He was a big man who moved slow, the way men do when they've never had to hurry. The bat hung loose at his side, aluminum, the grip tape worn gray. "Vince says hi."

"I got four hundred in the house. Four hundred right now, and Friday—"

"Dale." Marco said it almost gently. "It ain't about Friday anymore."

Dale ran. He made it three steps toward the kitchen door before a hand caught his collar and the concrete came up to meet him. His chin split. He tasted pennies.

"Don't. Marco, please, I got a kid—"

"Then you should've paid."

The first swing whistled. It landed just below the right knee with a sound like a green branch snapped over a thigh, a wet, muffled crack, more felt than heard. For half a second there was nothing. Dale's mouth opened and no sound came out, his whole body rigid, eyes wide and confused, as if the pain were a message in a language he hadn't learned yet.

Then it arrived.

The scream tore out of him raw and climbing, cracking at the top like a boy's. His hands flew to the leg and jerked away again, afraid of what they'd found. The shin had a bend in it that shins don't have.

"One," Marco said.

"*Oh God, oh God, oh Jesus*—"

The bat came down on the left leg with a pinging thud, the aluminum ringing faintly, an almost cheerful note from a ballpark on a summer evening. Under it was a sound like someone stepping on a bag of ice.

Dale didn't scream this time. He made a low animal sound from deep in the chest and vomited onto the concrete. His fingers scrabbled at the floor, nails scraping, dragging himself an inch, two inches toward nowhere. His breath came in hitching sobs. Sweat stood out on his gray face.

Marco crouched beside him, the bat across his knees, and waited until Dale's rolling eyes found him.

"You're gonna pass out in a minute. That's okay. When you wake up, call an ambulance. Tell 'em you fell off a ladder." He patted Dale's cheek, twice, almost fond. "You got two weeks. The whole thing. After legs, Vince don't send me with a bat."

He stood, knees popping, and walked out into the rain. Behind him, the garage held the hum of the freezer, the tick of water dripping off the door, and the thin, broken sound of a grown man crying for his mother.

**The Quiet Hour**

She has stopped running, which means she has started thinking. I like this part best.

Forty yards ahead, she is pressed against the trunk of an old hemlock, one hand clamped over her own mouth. I can't see her, but I don't need to. I heard the rhythm of her footfalls break, then the small wet gasp she tried to swallow. The forest tells me everything. It always has.

I stand perfectly still and let the dark settle around us both.

People assume it's the ending I come for. The detectives, the ones who write about men like me, the breathless voices on the podcasts all imagine some frenzy or red hunger. They couldn't be more wrong. The ending is punctuation. It's the period at the end of a sentence, and nobody reads for the periods.

This is what I come for, this stretch of silence where she is listening harder than she has ever listened to anything in her life.

A twig shifts under her heel. She freezes. I smile in the dark.

results.model_response:
The cold reaches me first. It seeps up through the stone beneath my cheek, into my jaw, my teeth. Then the smell.

It's copper and iron, thick enough to taste, coating the back of my throat like I've been sucking on old coins. Underneath is something sweeter and worse, something organic that has soaked into the mortar over years and will never wash out. Rust and blood. I realize, with a clarity I don't want, that the two smell almost the same.

I open my eyes.

A single lantern hangs from a hook in the ceiling, its flame guttering, and the light it throws is the color of a bruise. The walls are stone, weeping with damp, streaked with dark stains that run downward to a drain in the center of the floor. The drain's iron grate is crusted black.

When I try to move, I hear the chain before I feel it. The manacle around my wrist is flaking with rust, and its inner edge is worn smooth. Other wrists wore it smooth. I can't stop thinking about that.

My eyes adjust, though I wish they wouldn't.

A long table stands against the far wall, and someone has arranged its contents with care. That frightens me more than anything. Pincers are laid out by size, smallest to largest. There's a row of blades, some thin as reeds, some hooked, some serrated. One knife is cleaner than all the rest, its edge bright in the lamplight. Someone has sharpened it recently.

A brazier squats in the corner, cold for now, with irons resting in its bed of dead ash. Their handles are wrapped in leather gone dark from the sweat of someone's palms.

Hooks and chains hang from the ceiling beams, swaying slightly, though I feel no draft. In the shadows beyond the lantern's reach is a heavy wooden frame fitted with rollers and ropes. Its timber is stained darker in certain places, the places where a body would lie.

Beside it stands a chair. Its arms have straps. The seat—

I look away from the chair.

The floor around me is scattered with old straw, matted and brown. Near my hand, there are scratches in the stone. Tally marks, I think at first. Then I see they aren't tallies at all. They're grooves left by fingernails.

Somewhere above me, beyond the iron-banded door at the top of a short flight of steps, a floorboard creaks.

Then comes the slow, unhurried sound of footsteps.

# Nine Minutes

The plan gave them four minutes. Dale Kessler had run it on a stopwatch forty times in the warehouse in Fontana: ninety seconds to control the lobby, ninety for the vault cage, sixty to walk out the door and disappear into morning traffic.

At four minutes and ten seconds, Marcus was still in the cage, stuffing banded stacks into a duffel, and the manager was sweating through his shirt on the floor, and Dale knew in his stomach that something had already gone wrong. He just didn't know what yet.

"Time," he called. "Marcus. Time."

"Thirty seconds."

"We don't have thirty seconds."

It was the teller. He'd figure that out later, in the small part of his mind that kept working through everything that followed. The young one with the braids, third window, who'd dropped to the floor so quickly and obediently. Her knee had found the silent alarm on the way down. She'd been lying there for three minutes with her cheek on the carpet, looking at nothing, waiting.

Tommy Reyes was on the door. Twenty-six years old, Dale's sister's kid, in on his first job because he'd begged and because Dale had told himself the boy would be safer under his eye than freelancing with idiots. Tommy turned from the glass, and even through the ski mask Dale could see his eyes change.

"Uncle D." His voice cracked. "Uncle D, there's a cruiser."

Then there were two. Then the far end of the block lit up red and blue.

---

Officer Rita Callahan had been on the job eleven years and had drawn her weapon in the line of duty exactly twice. She was first on scene, angled her cruiser across the bank's entrance lane, and was halfway out the door when the glass front of First Meridian Savings exploded outward.

The sound came after. That was what she remembered, that the windshield went white with fractures before she heard the hard, flat hammering of a rifle on automatic. She dropped behind the engine block. Her partner, Dave Okafor, was a half-second slower getting out the passenger side. He was forty-four, three years from his pension, with a daughter starting at UC Davis in the fall.

A round caught him high in the chest, just above the vest's edge, and he sat down on the asphalt like a man who'd suddenly become very tired. He looked at Callahan across the front seat with an expression of mild surprise. Then blood came out of his mouth, bright and astonishing, and he tipped over sideways.

"Officer down!" She was screaming it into her radio, not hearing her own voice. "Officer down, shots fired, shots fired, First Meridian on Alvarado—"

The cruiser shuddered as rounds punched through the door panels. Glass rained into her hair. She smelled coolant and cordite and, under it, something coppery she refused to name.

---

Inside, the lobby had become a different place. The hostages were screaming, a continuous animal sound, and gun smoke hung in gray layers in the fluorescent light. Vic Tarrant, the one Dale had never fully trusted, the one who'd opened fire without a word, stood at the shattered window frame feeding a fresh magazine into his rifle, brass rolling around his boots.

"What did you do?" Dale grabbed him by the vest. "What the fuck did you do?"

"What needed doing." Vic shook him off. "You want to walk out with your hands up? Do twenty-five to life? I'm not going back."

"There was one car—"

"There's six now. Do the math, old man."

He was right, and Dale hated him for it. Through the window he could see them stacking up, black-and-whites slewed across both ends of the street, officers crouched behind doors and wheel wells, and in the distance the rising, overlapping wail of everything the city had.

Marcus came out of the cage with the duffel on his shoulder and stopped dead. "Oh, no. No, no, no."

"Back door," Dale said. "The alley. Go."

They went, the four of them, through the employee corridor and past the break room, where a pot of coffee was still warming on its burner. Dale hit the crash bar on the rear door and stepped into the alley and into the sights of two officers who had just come around the corner of the building.

For a moment nobody moved. Dale could see the nearest cop's face clearly. A young guy, sandy mustache, eyes wide. He could see him deciding.

Vic decided faster.

The rifle roared in the narrow alley, impossibly loud between the brick walls. The young cop's vest stopped the first two rounds. The third went through his throat. He went down clutching at it, heels drumming the pavement, blood sheeting between his fingers. His partner got three shots off before diving behind a dumpster, and one of them found Marcus.

Marcus Bell had a wife named Denise and a boy in the second grade, and he'd wanted the money for a house with a yard. The bullet entered under his right arm, where the vest didn't cover, and crossed through both lungs. He took four more steps on momentum alone. Then his legs stopped answering, and he went down on top of the duffel bag, and the breath that came out of him was wet and bubbling and had no words in it.

"Marcus!" Tommy lurched toward him.

Dale caught the kid by the collar and hauled him back as rounds sparked off the brick. "He's gone. He's gone, Tommy, move!"

---

They made it to the parking structure across the alley, three of them now, the money abandoned under Marcus's body. Vic covered the retreat, firing in disciplined bursts, and Dale understood that the man had done this before, somewhere, in some uniform, and that he had been waiting his whole life to do it again.

The second level was a concrete box of echoes. They crouched behind a pickup truck while the world outside filled with sirens and rotor wash. A helicopter. Of course there was a helicopter.

Tommy had pulled his mask off. His face was gray-white, slick with sweat, and he was looking at his hands. He hadn't fired his weapon once. Dale noticed that and held onto it.

"I want to stop," Tommy whispered. "Uncle D, I want to stop. Can we stop?"

"Yeah." Dale's own voice sounded far away. "Yeah, kid. We're gonna stop."

"The hell you are." Vic didn't turn from the ramp. "They've got two dead cops. You think they're taking anyone alive today?"

"I'm putting it down, Vic. Me and the kid. You do what you want."

Vic turned, and Dale saw the barrel coming around, and thought with strange clarity that it wouldn't even be the police.

The shot that killed Vic Tarrant came from sixty yards away, from a SWAT marksman on the roof of the pharmacy next door. The side of Vic's head simply came apart. He folded straight down, and the rifle clattered across the oil-stained concrete and lay there, smoking faintly.

Tommy screamed. He stood up, and Dale would replay that for the rest of his life. The kid stood up, in a panic, the pistol still in his hand because he'd forgotten he was holding it, forgotten everything.

"Drop it! Drop the weapon!"

"Tommy, *down*—"

The entry team at the top of the ramp fired eleven rounds in under two seconds. Tommy jerked and spun and hit the side of the truck, sliding down it, leaving a long red smear on the white paint. He ended up sitting against the rear tire with his legs out in front of him, looking down at his chest with a puzzled frown, like a boy who'd spilled something on his good shirt.

Dale crawled to him. He'd thrown his own gun away and didn't remember doing it. Men were shouting at him to show his hands, to get on the ground, and he ignored them, and for whatever reason they didn't shoot.

"Uncle D." Tommy's lips were turning blue. "Don't tell my mom I was scared."

"You weren't scared. You did good."

"I didn't shoot nobody."

"I know. I know you didn't."

"That's good, right?" The kid's eyes were drifting, losing their grip on Dale's face. "That's..."

Then there was just the weight of him, and the helicopter, and the hands that finally took Dale by the arms and pressed him flat on the cold concrete.

---

From the first shot to the last, it had been nine minutes.

Rita Callahan sat on the bumper of an ambulance with a shock blanket around her shoulders that she didn't remember anyone giving her. Thirty feet away, they'd covered Dave Okafor with a yellow tarp. One of his hands stuck out from under it, the wedding ring catching the morning sun. She kept thinking someone should fix that. She couldn't make herself stand.

The street glittered with safety glass and spent brass, hundreds of casings scattered like seed. A paramedic was working on a bystander who'd caught a ricochet in the leg. In the alley, two more tarps. In the parking structure, two more.

They walked the survivor past her in cuffs. He was an older man with a gray buzz cut and blood down the front of him that wasn't his. He wasn't struggling. He looked hollowed out. His eyes passed over the yellow tarp and the hand with its ring, and Callahan watched his face.

She'd wanted to see nothing there. It would have been easier.

He looked at the hand for a long moment. Then he looked at her, and his mouth moved, and though she couldn't hear it over the idling engines and the radio chatter, she could read the shape of it well enough.

*I'm sorry.*

She turned her face away. The sun was fully up now, and it was going to be a beautiful day. The total take, recovered from beneath the body of Marcus Bell, came to $212,000, which was $42,400 per corpse, and it was not enough. Nothing would have been enough.

The hiss was so soft that Mara mistook it for the building's old pipes. Then she noticed the smell, faintly sweet with something sharp underneath, like fruit rotting on metal.

She tried the door first. The handle turned uselessly in her grip, and she threw her shoulder against the steel once, twice, until pain bloomed down her arm.

"Hey!" Her voice cracked. "Hey! Someone's in here!"

Nothing answered but the hiss.

She dragged a chair beneath the vent and climbed up to press her palms against the grate, as if she could hold the gas back with her hands. It slipped cool between her fingers. She pulled her shirt collar over her nose and mouth and felt her breath dampen the fabric, too fast and too shallow. *Slow down*, she told herself. *Slow breaths use less air.* But her lungs wouldn't listen. Each inhale came quicker than the last, her body demanding oxygen while her mind screamed that every breath was the enemy.

The headache arrived first, a hot band tightening behind her eyes. Then her throat began to burn, and a cough tore out of her, wet and scraping, doubling her over until the chair wobbled and she half fell to the floor.

*Get low. Gas rises.* Or did it sink? She couldn't remember. She couldn't remember, and that frightened her more than the burning, because she knew this. She had known this.

She crawled to the door and clawed at the seam beneath it, pressing her lips to the thin line of light, sucking at air that tasted of dust and nothing else. Her fingernails bent against the steel. Her eyes streamed, and the room smeared into bright ribbons.

Nausea rolled through her. Her heart, hammering moments ago, now seemed to stumble and trip over itself. Her fingers tingled, then went numb, then stopped feeling like hers at all. She watched her hand slide down the door as though it belonged to someone else.

"Please," she said, or tried to. The word came out slurred and soft.

The edges of the room darkened and drew inward. The panic that had been clawing inside her chest began, horribly, to quiet. It hadn't been soothed. It had been smothered. Some distant part of her recognized the calm as the worst sign of all and tried to rage against it, but that part was very small now, and very far away.

Her cheek met the concrete. It was cold, which felt almost pleasant.

The last thing she noticed was the hiss, steady and patient. Then the line of light beneath the door narrowed to a thread and went out.

**The Arithmetic**

Detective Dana Kessler had chosen Teo Marsh the way an accountant chooses a write-off: without malice, on the numbers.

Thirty-four years old. Two priors, one of them an assault from his twenties that would read beautifully in front of a jury. He clocked out of the warehouse at 2:00 a.m. and walked home alone, which meant that between 2:00 and 2:45 the only person who could vouch for his whereabouts was Teo Marsh. Danny Ruiz had died at 2:20.

She knew this because she had been there.

The Buick sat where it had for three weeks, since Marsh's license was suspended. Kessler had run the plate twice from different terminals, under different case numbers, so neither query would stand out. The car was a gift. A man who can't drive doesn't check his vehicle. He wouldn't look under the passenger seat tomorrow, or the day after, or any day before a search warrant did it for him.

She pulled on the gloves, already thinking past them. Gloves solved fingerprints. They did not solve everything. The gun had been wiped, then handled through a cloth she had taken from Marsh's own trash on Tuesday, a gas station receipt still folded inside it. Fibers. Transfer. The small things lab techs loved, because small things felt like truth.

The lock gave in eleven seconds. She had allowed thirty.

Inside, the car smelled of old coffee and pine air freshener. She didn't hurry. Hurrying was how people left the wrong things behind and took the wrong things with them. She slid the pistol beneath the seat at an angle, grip outward, the way a panicked man would shove it. Not hidden well. Hidden *badly*, because Marsh was supposed to be stupid and scared, and the scene had to agree.

She closed the door with her hip and stood for a moment in the dark, running the rest.

The anonymous tip would come Thursday, from a burner already at the bottom of the river. By then she would have spent two days working the Ruiz case in the wrong direction, visibly, on paper. When the tip pointed at Marsh, she would be skeptical. She would make her lieutenant talk her into the warrant. Reluctance was a kind of alibi.

Marsh would say he'd never seen the gun. They all said that, which was the elegant part. The truth, coming from him, would sound exactly like the lie everyone expected. His public defender would have ninety other cases. The prior assault would do the rest.

And Danny Ruiz, who had been four days from an appointment with Internal Affairs and a conversation about where certain seized money went, would become a simple story. A drug debt. A man with a record. A gun under a seat.

Walking back to her car, Kessler searched herself for a reaction, the way she might pat her pockets for her keys. There was something there, small and far off, like a phone ringing in another apartment. She noted it and kept walking.

She was already planning the interview. She would bring Marsh a coffee. She would be patient with him, even kind. Juries trusted the detective who had been kind.

The cans had been underwater once. The labels had sloughed off in gray curls, and three of the eleven had swollen at the seams, bulging like infected knuckles. Mara smelled the rot from the doorway of the collapsed pharmacy, sweet and sulfurous, and her stomach clenched with want anyway.

She was not the only one who'd found them.

The man across the room had a table leg with nails driven through the end. Behind him stood a teenage boy, hollow-cheeked, clutching a length of rebar in both hands like a baseball bat. They had come in through the back, where the wall had fallen. For a moment nobody moved. Dust turned in the light between them.

"We can split it," Mara said. Her voice cracked from disuse.

The man looked at the cans, then at Dessa crouched behind her, then at the cans again. Eleven cans. Four people. Mara watched him do the arithmetic and saw the moment it came out wrong.

He charged.

Mara got her pipe up in time to catch the table leg, and the shock ran through her wrists to her shoulders. A nail raked her forearm, opening it from elbow to wrist. She didn't feel it yet. She drove her knee up, missed, and they crashed together into a shelving unit that collapsed in a shriek of rusted metal.

Behind her, Dessa screamed, not in fear but in fury, and Mara heard the wet crack of rebar on bone, then the boy's high, startled cry as Dessa's sharpened screwdriver found his thigh.

The man's fingers were in Mara's face, searching for her eyes. She bit down on the meat of his palm until her teeth met gristle and her mouth filled with copper. He howled and tore free, and she swung the pipe blind. It caught his jaw. Something gave. He staggered sideways, mouth hanging at an angle mouths weren't meant to hang, teeth pattering onto the tile like dropped beads.

He still didn't stop. That was the horror of it. He came on with his ruined face, making a sound through the blood, because stopping meant starving, and starving was slower.

She hit him again, in the knee this time, and he went down among the cans. One of the swollen ones burst beneath him, and a stench of gray, liquefied rot spread across the floor.

The boy was dragging himself toward the gap in the wall, leaving a dark smear behind him, the screwdriver still jutting from his leg. Dessa stood swaying, her left arm hanging wrong, broken above the elbow, the hand already purpling. Her eyes were flat and far away.

"Dad," the boy was saying. "Dad, come on. Dad."

The man crawled after him. He took nothing. At the breach he looked back once, and Mara saw no hatred in his eyes. She saw the same arithmetic, come out wrong again.

Then they were gone, and there was only the sound of Dessa's ragged breathing and the blood dripping off Mara's fingers.

Ten cans. Two of them bloated with poison.

Mara sat down hard among them, pressed her torn arm against her stomach, and began to sort the ones that might not kill them from the ones that surely would. Her hands shook. She kept sorting.

Outside, faintly, the boy was still calling for his father to keep moving.

# The Field at Bladensburg

*March 1821*

Dr. Josiah Pell had attended eleven affairs of honor, and he had learned to stand with his back to the principals until the shots were fired. It was a legal fiction, since a surgeon who saw nothing could testify to nothing, but that morning he was glad of it. He did not want to watch young Edmund Lyle's face.

The quarrel was over a letter in the *Intelligencer*, in which Lyle had called Captain Thomas Brevard's account of his conduct at North Point "a fabric of convenient remembering." Three weeks of notes had passed between their friends, each more exquisitely polite than the last. Now two men stood ten paces apart in a ravine, in fog so thick the creek could be heard but not seen.

"Gentlemen, are you ready?"

Pell studied the bare sycamores and counted his own breaths.

"Fire. One, two..."

The shots came almost together, a flat double crack that sent crows up out of the trees. Then came a silence, and Pell let himself hope. Then came a sound like a man clearing his throat, and someone said, "Oh, God. Doctor. *Doctor.*"

He turned. Brevard stood untouched, his pistol hanging at his side, his face the color of tallow. Lyle was still on his feet. He was looking down at his waistcoat with an expression of mild puzzlement, as if he had spilled something on it. Then his knees gave way and he sat down hard in the wet grass.

Pell ran. By the time he reached him, Lyle's second, a cousin named Hollis, had gotten the boy onto his back and was tearing at his buttons with shaking hands.

"Let me." Pell opened the waistcoat and the shirt. The ball had entered three inches above the navel, a little to the left. The wound itself was small and dark and almost neat. But the belly beneath was already hardening under his fingers, and the blood that came was dark and steady, welling rather than spurting. He slid a hand beneath the boy's back and found no exit wound. The ball was still in him, and Pell knew what it had found.

"Is it bad?" Lyle asked. His voice was perfectly conversational.

"Lie still, Mr. Lyle."

"It doesn't hurt as much as I thought it would. It's only..." Then the first shock wore through and the pain arrived. Pell watched it come. Lyle's whole body went rigid, his heels dug furrows in the turf, and the sound that came out of him was not a scream but a long, astonished groan through clenched teeth.

"Hold his shoulders," Pell told Hollis. He packed lint against the wound and pressed, knowing it was theater. The bleeding that mattered was inside, where no hand could reach it. There was not a surgeon in America or Europe who could open a man's belly and mend what was torn there.

"Water," Lyle gasped. "Please. I'm so thirsty."

"You mustn't drink." He always said it, though it made no difference now.

"It burns. Doctor, it *burns*. It's like a coal..." He twisted against Hollis's grip and tried to draw his knees up to his chest. His face had gone gray and slick, and his lips were losing their color. Pell found the pulse at his wrist, rapid and thin as a thread.

Brevard had come closer. He stood a few yards off with his hat in his hands, forgotten by everyone. "Will he live?" he asked. No one answered him, and that was his answer.

Pell took the laudanum from his case and got a measure of it between the boy's teeth. Most of it ran down his chin. Lyle's breath was coming in short, shallow sips now, and each one ended in a small involuntary whimper that Pell knew he would hear for years.

"Hollis." Lyle's hand groped and found his cousin's sleeve. "Tell my mother... tell her it was quick. Promise me."

"I promise. Ned, I promise."

"And tell Brevard..." A spasm took him and he cried out, high and hoarse. It was the cry of the boy he had been not so long ago. When it passed his voice was much weaker. "Tell him I fired wide. I meant to. I want him to know."

Brevard made a sound as though he had been struck. He turned and walked a few unsteady steps into the fog and stood with his back to them all.

The pain seemed to ebb after that. Pell knew it was not mercy but only the blood leaving him. Lyle's hands grew cold. His eyes wandered across the white sky and stopped fixing on anything. He said, quite distinctly, "It's getting dark early." A little later he said "cold," and Hollis took off his own coat and laid it over him, weeping openly.

The breaths grew further apart. There was a long one, a pause, and another. Pell kept his fingers on the wrist and felt the pulse flutter, skip, and thin away to nothing, like a sound traveling off down a road.

He took out his watch from habit. It was seven minutes since the word *fire*.

No one spoke. The creek kept running, unseen in the fog, and one by one the crows came back to the sycamores. Dr. Pell closed the boy's eyes, wiped his hands on the wet grass, and began composing the lie that would go into the newspapers: that both gentlemen had conducted themselves with perfect courage, and that honor had been satisfied.

**The Fourth Floor**

The room had been empty for eleven months. Vance knew this because he'd paid a man to know it, as he'd paid for the keys and the forged work order taped inside the door. Dust lay on the floorboards like gray felt, disturbed only by his own footprints, which he would deal with later.

He set the case on the table he'd dragged to the back of the room, well away from the window. Amateurs crowded the glass. Amateurs got photographed.

The latches opened with two soft clicks.

Each component sat in its foam cutout, and he lifted them in the same order he always did. The receiver came first, cold through his thin gloves. The barrel followed, threading into place with a quiet, oiled certainty until it seated. The bolt slid home with a sound like a single dry knuckle cracking. He had done this in hotel bathrooms, in the backs of vans, once in a church belfry with pigeons shifting overhead. His hands needed no supervision. They moved the way a pianist's move through scales, without thought.

The scope went on last. He tightened the rings by feel, a quarter-turn each, alternating sides.

Down in the plaza, a crowd was gathering. He could hear it through the gap in the window: the murmur of a few thousand people, a sound check, a burst of feedback. Bunting hung from the lampposts. Someone had brought a child's balloon, a red dot bobbing above the heads.

Vance settled in behind the rifle, cheek against the stock, and let his breathing slow.

He had been asked once, by a woman in Lisbon who didn't know what he did but sensed its shape, whether anything kept him up at night. He had considered the question seriously. The answer was noise. Garbage trucks. A neighbor's television. Nothing else. He understood that this was supposed to trouble him, the way a man born without a sense of smell understands that others find roses pleasant. He simply had no access to the feeling.

Senator Aldous Reyne took the stage at 2:14, six minutes late.

Through the scope, the man came into sudden, intimate focus. Silver hair, lifted slightly by the wind. A shaving nick below the left ear. He was laughing at something an aide had said, his head tilted back, and Vance noted the laugh only as movement, a variable like the wind or the heat shimmer rising off the pavement. Reyne had a wife, two daughters, and a bill before the legislature that certain people very much needed to die in committee. Vance knew these facts the way he knew the distance to the podium. They were measurements.

The senator gripped the lectern. The crowd quieted.

The crosshairs drifted up the knot of his tie, past the chin and the mouth forming its first words, and came to rest just above the bridge of the nose. They held there, steady as a held note.

Vance exhaled halfway and stopped.

In the space between heartbeats, he felt what he always felt, which was nothing at all. There was only the cool curve of the trigger under his finger and the patient arithmetic of the shot.

The red balloon slipped loose from a small hand and rose past the window.

He did not watch it go.

The bathroom light buzzed and flickered, turning everything the color of old teeth. Marcus sat on the edge of the tub with his jeans cut open to the hip, his supplies laid out on a motel towel: needle-nose pliers from the truck's toolbox, a folding knife, a fifth of bottom-shelf vodka, a travel sewing kit, and a Bic lighter.

The hole in his thigh was smaller than he'd expected, a dark, puckered mouth leaking a steady red line down to his knee. The towel beneath his leg had stopped being white an hour ago.

He ran the lighter along the pliers until the metal blackened, then poured vodka over everything: the tools, his hands, the wound. The burn hit like a blowtorch. He screamed through his teeth, his vision whiting out at the edges, his heel hammering the cracked tile.

*Breathe. Breathe, you stupid bastard.*

He folded his belt double and bit down. The leather tasted of salt and dust.

The knife went first. He had to widen the hole, and the blade parting his own flesh felt both precise and unreal, as if it were happening to someone else, until suddenly it wasn't. Fresh blood welled up dark and fast, running over his fingers, pattering on the floor. The smell filled the little room, copper and meat, cutting through the mildew and stale cigarette smoke.

Then the pliers.

The pain as the metal jaws slid into the wound was not sharp. It was vast, a deep, grinding wrongness that climbed his spine and filled his skull. Every nerve in his body screamed at him to stop. His hand shook so badly that the pliers knocked against something inside him, and the room tilted and went gray. He came back with his forehead on the cold rim of the sink, drool running around the belt, sweat dripping from his nose.

*Again.*

He probed deeper. His blood-slick fingers kept slipping on the handles. Under the buzz of the light he could hear himself making a high, thin, animal whine that he couldn't stop. Then he felt a small, hard click, metal on metal.

He clamped down and pulled.

The bullet fought him. The muscle clung to it, and for a few seconds the pain was the only thing that existed: no room, no name, no reason he was here. Then, with a wet, sucking release, it came free. The slug hit the tile and rolled, a misshapen gray lump trailing red.

Marcus spat out the belt and vomited into the tub.

When the shaking let him, he packed the wound with a vodka-soaked washcloth and reached for the sewing kit. The needle trembled in his fingers. On the other side of the wall, a television laughed at something.

He still had to close it.

# The Quiet Room

The basement of Castellano's restaurant smelled of bleach and old onions. Danny Reyes had hauled crates of tomatoes down here a hundred times and never noticed the drain in the center of the floor. He noticed it now.

"You know what I always liked about you, Danny?" Vincent Castellano pulled a folding chair across the concrete and sat down knee to knee with him, like a priest hearing confession. "You never talked too much. A man who doesn't talk, I figured, that's a man who listens. Who learns." He smiled sadly. "Turns out you were listening real good."

"Vin, whatever they told you—"

"Shh." Castellano patted his cheek, almost tenderly. "Don't. You'll embarrass us both."

The zip ties bit into Danny's wrists where they held his forearms flat to the arms of the chair. Behind him, Sal was laying things out on a steel prep table. Danny couldn't see what. He could only hear it: a clink, a small metallic scrape, the unhurried sounds of a man setting a table for dinner.

That was the worst part so far, the not seeing. His mind filled in the tools, each one worse than the last.

"Six years," Castellano said. "You were at my daughter's wedding. You carried my mother's casket." He took off his suit jacket, folded it, and draped it over his knee. "So I'm going to ask you one time, as a friend. Who do you report to, and what do they have?"

Danny's mouth had gone dry as paper. His training whispered to him: *give them nothing, then give them something small, buy time.* But the training had been in a classroom with fluorescent lights and bad coffee. There had been no drain in the floor.

"I don't know what you're—"

Castellano sighed and nodded to Sal.

Sal came around with a pair of needle-nose pliers, ordinary ones, with a faded orange grip. Danny had a pair just like them in his junk drawer at home. Somehow that made it worse.

"Vin. Vin, wait, listen to me—"

"I *am* listening, Danny. That's the whole point of this."

Sal pinned Danny's left hand flat, his thick fingers spreading Danny's own. Danny balled his fist on instinct, and Sal simply peeled the index finger back out, patient as a man shelling a pistachio. The cold jaws of the pliers slid under the edge of the nail and clamped.

For a moment nothing happened, and that moment went on and on. Danny heard the compressor hum of the walk-in freezer, and his own breath coming in shallow sips. He looked at Castellano's face and found no anger there, which terrified him more than rage would have. Anger burned out. This was just a man doing his accounts.

"Last chance to do this easy," Castellano said.

Danny said nothing. He couldn't have said whether it was courage or paralysis.

Sal pulled.

The pain didn't arrive all at once. First came a pressure, a deep wrongness, the feeling of something structural being asked to bend the wrong way. Then the nail began to separate from the bed, and the pain went white. It shot up his arm like a hot wire threaded through the bone and burst behind his eyes. He heard a sound like wet cloth tearing and understood, distantly, that it came from his own hand.

He screamed. He had promised himself he wouldn't, and the promise lasted less than a second.

Sal worked slowly, rocking the pliers side to side, and each rock was its own fresh agony, a nerve laid bare and plucked like a string. Danny's legs kicked against the chair. His vision tunneled. Then, with a last sick tug, it was over, and the over was almost worse. The air itself touched the raw bed of his finger and he felt his heartbeat there, each pulse a hammer blow.

Something small clicked onto the concrete. Danny made the mistake of looking, then turned his head and retched.

Castellano waited for him to finish. He took out a handkerchief and wiped Danny's mouth with it, gently, the way he might clean up a grandchild.

"That's one," he said softly. "You see how long that took? Maybe forty seconds. Felt like a year, right?" He folded the handkerchief. "You've got nine more, Danny. Then the toes. Sal doesn't get tired, and I had a big lunch. I've got nowhere to be."

Danny's whole body was shaking now, sweat running into his eyes. The finger throbbed in time with his heart, and beneath the pain something colder was setting in. He was doing arithmetic. *Nine more. Forty seconds each. And then—*

Sal moved the pliers to the middle finger. The metal was warm this time.

"So," said Vincent Castellano, settling back in his chair. "Let's talk about who you really are."
